I’ve seen a lot of people asking how @RialoHQ transactions can run onchain, jump offchain for a bit, and then resume execution like nothing happened.

From the outside, it almost feels like magic. But under the hood, it’s a very intentional design built around privacy preserving asynchronous transactions. Instead of forcing all computation and data to live onchain, Rialo allows smart contracts to initiate encrypted requests, temporarily suspend execution, and wait for offchain responses all without breaking determinism or trust assumptions.

When a user submits a transaction, the smart contract executes normally until it reaches a point where external data is required for example, a Web2 API like a FICO score. At that moment, Rialo records the request onchain in encrypted form and safely suspends execution. The request is then handled offchain inside an end to end encrypted environment, ensuring that sensitive data is never exposed to the mempool, validators, or MEV bots. No raw data is bridged onchain, no oracle style data dumping just secure, private computation happening exactly where it should.

Once the offchain computation completes, Rialo resumes the original smart contract via an encrypted callback in a later block. Execution continues seamlessly, preserving onchain guarantees while benefiting from offchain flexibility. To developers, this feels incredibly natural almost like using async/await or continuations in Web2 systems. And that’s the real breakthrough: Rialo doesn’t force Web3 devs to relearn everything from scratch. It brings familiar async patterns into blockchain execution, unlocking privacy first, real world use cases like identity, credit scoring, and enterprise integrations the way smart contracts were always meant to work.

RISC-V keeps compilation simple and bounded, reducing attack surface while staying fast. Fewer layers, clearer behavior, easier verification.

What Can Break This Design?

Every system that introduces structure also introduces new points of failure.
Designing responsibility doesn’t eliminate risk. It relocates it.
So the right question now is not whether Rialo’s design is elegant —

but where it could fail.
------------------------------------------------------------
Failure Point #1 — Responsibility Becomes a Bottleneck
When responsibility has an address, that address can become overloaded.

If too many decisions, checks, or conditions depend on a single structural layer, latency increases and flexibility decreases.
A system meant to prevent chaos can quietly turn into a choke point.

Structure protects — until it slows.
------------------------------------------------------------
Failure Point #2 — Over-Constraint Kills Adoption
Clear boundaries create clarity.
But boundaries that are too strict can discourage experimentation.

Builders may ask:

- “Is this worth integrating with?”

- “Are the constraints too heavy?”
- “Can I move fast enough here?”
If responsibility costs too much upfront, developers may simply choose looser systems.
Clarity without adoption is still failure.

------------------------------------------------------------

Failure Point #3 — Assumptions About the Real World
@RialoHQ's design assumes something important:
That real-world workflows can be expressed in structured conditions.

But reality is messy.

Data is incomplete. Signals are delayed. Human behavior is unpredictable.
If the system expects the world to be cleaner than it is, responsibility becomes brittle instead of robust.

------------------------------------------------------------
Failure Point #4 — Governance Re-enters Through the Back Door
Even well-designed responsibility structures eventually face edge cases.

When rules fail to cover reality, someone has to decide.
If those decisions fall back to:
- ad-hoc governance
- social consensus

- emergency intervention
Then responsibility quietly shifts again — away from structure, back to people.

This isn’t wrong. But it must be acknowledged.
------------------------------------------------------------
Closing — Strength Is Knowing Where You Can Break
Strong systems aren’t those that claim to be unbreakable.

They’re the ones that are honest about how they might fail.
@RialoHQ's approach raises the bar by making responsibility explicit.

The next step isn’t more belief.
It’s testing:
- where the structure bends
- where it cracks
- and whether it fails gracefully

That’s what determines whether design becomes infrastructure.

Why Rialo’s Privacy Strategy Is About Combination, Not a Single Solution
The REX Stack: Integrating MPC, FHE, and TEE — and the Significance of Jan Camenisch

Privacy in blockchain has long been discussed as a competition between individual technologies.
Is zero-knowledge fast enough?
Is fully homomorphic encryption simply too slow?
Do trusted execution environments introduce excessive trust assumptions?
Rialo reframes the question entirely.
In a blockchain designed to connect directly with the real world (Web2), no single privacy technology can realistically satisfy all requirements.
Different threat models, performance constraints, and regulatory conditions must coexist within the same system.
This perspective led to the design of Rialo’s REX stack — a privacy execution layer that combines MPC, FHE, and TEE based on their intended roles rather than treating any one of them as a universal solution.

The Core Principle of the REX Stack:

The Right Technology, in the Right Place
REX does not present any cryptographic primitive as a one-size-fits-all answer.
Instead, privacy technologies are selected based on which trust assumptions and performance costs are acceptable at each execution stage.

Multi-Party Computation (MPC) is used in scenarios that require collaborative computation among multiple parties — such as key management, distributed data processing, and joint computations.
By removing dependence on a single operator, MPC becomes a practical choice for workflows that integrate with existing Web2 services.

Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) is reserved for high-security contexts where data must remain encrypted throughout computation.
While computationally expensive, FHE offers an unmatched guarantee: computation without decryption.
Rialo avoids forcing FHE into a general-purpose execution environment, instead applying it selectively to limited, high-value operations where its security properties justify the cost.

Trusted Execution Environments (TEE) are used at the interface with the external world — API calls, legacy infrastructure, and real-time processing.
Although TEEs do not provide a fully trustless model, they offer a pragmatic balance between security and performance, making them well-suited for Web2-native connectivity.

The strength of REX lies not in using all three technologies simultaneously, but in clearly defining when each technology should — and should not — be used.

What Jan Camenisch’s Appointment Signals

Rialo’s decision to bring on Jan Camenisch — a former IBM researcher and a leading figure in anonymous credentials and privacy-enhancing technologies (PETs) — carries significance beyond symbolic credibility.
Throughout his career, Camenisch has focused less on what is theoretically possible and more on what can be sustained in real-world systems over time.

This philosophy aligns closely with Rialo’s approach:
Treating privacy as core infrastructure, not an optional feature
Designing cryptographic systems with regulatory and enterprise environments in mind

Prioritizing standardization and long-term extensibility over short-term demonstrations
His involvement signals that Rialo aims to move beyond experimental research and toward a privacy architecture designed for practical deployment.

Structural Differentiation: Beyond Technology Maximalism

Many privacy-focused projects are built around a single dominant technique:

FHE-centric chains offer strong confidentiality but struggle with performance constraints

TEE-based systems achieve high throughput at the cost of concentrated trust assumptions

MPC networks distribute trust effectively but introduce coordination and operational complexity

Rialo does not frame these approaches as inferior.
Instead, it treats privacy as an execution-layer concern, allowing different technologies to be combined depending on the use case.

This architectural choice enables:

Direct integration with Web2 services

Privacy controls that adapt to regulatory requirements

Flexible trade-offs between security, performance, and trust assumptions

Rather than claiming technological superiority, Rialo differentiates itself through a design philosophy grounded in real-world operating conditions.

Closing Thoughts

The REX stack does not promise perfect or absolute privacy.
Its goal is more pragmatic: to expand the range of privacy that can realistically be applied in production environments.

The combination of Jan Camenisch’s expertise,
the selective deployment of MPC, FHE, and TEE,
and a design explicitly built for Web2 connectivity

suggests that Rialo is exploring the next phase of privacy-focused blockchains —
not as an abstract ideal, but as a system-level engineering challenge aimed at real-world use.
In that sense, Rialo’s most defining characteristic may be its willingness to treat privacy not as an ideology, but as a problem of system design.

The real challenge in blockchain execution is timing, not throughput

Most discussions about blockchain performance focus on how much a system can process.

But in practice, systems fail not because they are too slow,
but because they act at the wrong time.

Too early, and state isn’t final.
Too late, and users experience delays, retries, or missed outcomes.

This is where execution models quietly define everything.

Traditional chains wait.
They wait for transactions.
They wait for callers.
They wait for bots to notice something changed.

That makes execution reactive by design.

Modern systems try to compensate with parallelism.
But parallel execution only shifts the problem:
now the system must decide when conflicts are acceptable
and when it must pause.

Assume conflicts are rare, and you move fast—until you don’t.
Assume conflicts are common, and you stay safe—by waiting.

The important insight is this:
execution quality is revealed when assumptions break.

Under load.
Under contention.
Under real-world timing constraints.

This is why performance is not a single metric.
It’s how gracefully execution degrades
when reality does not behave as expected.

Rialo treats execution as a continuous process,
not a series of isolated requests.

Time progresses.
State evolves.
Conditions mature.

Execution is not something you trigger.
It’s something the system is already prepared for.

Correctness comes from knowing when not to act,
and reliability comes from letting execution happen
only when the system is ready.

Blockchains don’t fail because they can’t move fast enough.
They fail because they don’t know when to move at all.

Execution design decides that.

Optimistic Execution and @RialoHQ's Conclusion: Maximizing Parallelism ⚡

When discussing parallel execution, the key lever for increasing blockchain throughput, we inevitably encounter the Optimistic Execution model, which breaks through the limitations of traditional approaches🚀

Optimistic execution starts from a fundamentally opposite assumption to pessimistic execution.

➜ Its core premise is that most transactions operate on different states, and that actual conflicts are rare and exceptional events 🧠

As a result, optimistic execution does not block transactions before execution.

Under this model, transactions are executed immediately and in parallel, without entering a waiting state in advance.

In other words, there is no pre-execution phase where transactions are paused due to potential conflicts.

Instead, a validation step is performed after execution, just before commit. At this stage, the system checks whether the data used during transaction execution was modified by other transactions in the meantime.

If a state change is detected, the transaction’s result is invalidated and the transaction is re-executed. and if no conflict is found, the transaction is committed as-is, without any additional cost ✅

Ultimately, the cost in optimistic execution is not an ever-present waiting time that all transactions must bear, but a re-execution cost paid only when an actual conflict occurs 💸

This distinction is what Rialo considers most important.

➜ Optimistic execution does not ignore conflicts.
Rather, it treats conflicts as an integral part of the execution model and incurs costs only when they genuinely matter ⚖️

In this sense, optimistic execution is not a workaround that merely overlooks conflicts, but an efficient structure that embraces conflict potential as a natural aspect of execution and pays costs precisely at the points where issues arise.

As a result, in the vast majority of scenarios where conflicts are rare, parallelism can be pushed to its theoretical limits.

That said, this approach is not a silver bullet.
•  Write-heavy workloads: Conflicts become more frequent, increasing re-execution costs ✍️
•  Read-heavy workloads: High throughput and low latency can be achieved 📖

In conclusion, Rialo does not claim that one execution model is universally superior. Instead, it evaluates execution models based on how users actually interact with the blockchain and how data is accessed in practice 🧩

The trade-off lies between a pessimistic model that sacrifices some parallelism for stability, and an optimistic model that accepts conflicts in order to push performance to its limits.

[ The Transparency Paradox: Why Blockchains Need Secrets to Build Real Apps ]

Over the past fifteen years, the blockchain industry has pursued radical technological experiments driven by the ambitious vision of a trustless society.

Yet as of 2026, the reality of Web3 remains strikingly narrow compared to those promises.
The majority of what we call decentralized applications are still confined almost entirely to financial primitives such as decentralized exchanges and memecoin trading.
So called Real Apps like Stripe, Slack, or Notion, which depend on authentication, private data, and coordinated interaction with the real world, are virtually non existent within the ecosystem.

For a long time, the industry diagnosed this failure as a performance problem.
Bottlenecks were attributed to low transaction throughput and high gas fees, leading to an intense focus on faster and cheaper blockchains.

However, even with the emergence of high performance mainnets, the situation has not changed in any meaningful way.
This strongly suggests that the core limitation lies not in quantitative metrics, but in a deeper and more fundamental constraint called structural transparency.

Blockchains were designed to make all data public and all computation verifiable by anyone.
While this radical transparency is a strength for monetary systems, it becomes a fundamental liability at the application layer.

Real world software depends on secrets by default.

API keys, authentication credentials, private medical records, internal business logic, and proprietary algorithms are not optional components.
They are prerequisites.
Under the architecture of today’s public blockchains, placing a secret inside a smart contract is effectively the same as broadcasting it in plain text to the entire world.

Authenticated communication with external systems and the handling of sensitive user data therefore become fundamentally impossible.

As a result, smart contracts have become isolated artifacts that cannot log into external services or interact meaningfully with systems outside the chain.
At the same time, Web3 applications have collapsed into closed environments that can do little more than verify on chain balances and ownership.

Without the ability to manage credentials, identities, or private state, they are structurally incapable of supporting the workflows required by modern applications.

These limitations collide not only with technical realities, but also with legal and regulatory frameworks.

The Right to be Forgotten mandated by GDPR directly contradicts blockchain immutability.
To reduce legal risk, enterprises avoid placing personally identifiable information on chain altogether.

In an environment populated only by anonymous wallet addresses stripped of context, higher order services such as unsecured credit lending or insurance cannot emerge.

At a structural level, this creates a hard ceiling on what can be built on public blockchains.

Authentication requires secrets.
Access to real world data requires credentials.
Regulatory compliance requires controlled disclosure.

Without privacy, none of these conditions can be satisfied on chain.
Under these constraints, the path of least resistance for developers has been speculation oriented applications focused on trading and gambling mechanics.

As a result, blockchain has remained disconnected from the real economy and confined within a closed loop of financial experimentation.

This deadlock is not accidental.
It is the direct outcome of designing systems that can verify everything, but protect nothing.

A new generation of infrastructure has emerged to break this stalemate, and Rialo represents one such approach.
Rialo redefines blockchain architecture by treating privacy not as an add on or middleware component, but as a foundational property embedded directly at the protocol level.
By leveraging multi party computation and threshold signature schemes, Rialo manages sensitive information such as passwords and API keys by splitting them into cryptographic fragments.

No single node ever possesses the complete secret.
Even so, smart contracts are still able to perform authenticated interactions with external services.

This gives smart contracts a capability that was previously impossible.
They can securely access external APIs and interact with real world systems autonomously.

Beyond this, Rialo enables multiple parties to derive and cryptographically verify shared computational results without revealing their underlying private data.

This makes it possible to verify creditworthiness without exposing raw financial histories.
It also enables AI agents equipped with independent wallets and credentials to participate in autonomous economic activity.
Together, these primitives form the basis of a true machine economy.

Rialo also adopts an event driven architecture in which real world signals such as delivery confirmations or the fulfillment of off chain conditions can directly trigger blockchain transactions.

The result is a user experience closer to Web2, where blockchain logic operates quietly in the background rather than dominating the user interface.

For blockchain to evolve from a technical curiosity into the operating system of the real economy, the decisive question is not how much it can reveal.

The decisive question is what it can safely conceal.
Just as encrypted communication enabled the widespread adoption of e commerce and digital finance, blockchains can meaningfully integrate with the real world only once they possess native privacy.

The future suggested by projects like Rialo shows that privacy is not a tool for obscuring illicit behavior.
It is a foundational requirement for hosting genuine Real Apps.

We are now approaching a turning point, moving beyond speculative experimentation and toward the creation of tangible real world value built on secrets that are protected rather than exposed.

Why Rialo Chose RISC-V

Everyone just looks at TPS numbers when a new L1 drops, but Rialo hits different. They skipped the usual WASM or eBPF and went with RISC-V. Here is why this is a fundamentally game-changing decision.

1. The EVM is 256-bit, making the conversion process incredibly inefficient on our standard 64-bit computers. RISC-V, however, maps 1:1 with the hardware. With no middle steps, it is naturally faster and eliminates gas calculation errors.

2. Forcing proprietary languages or tools isolates an ecosystem. RISC-V natively supports standard tools like LLVM and Rust that developers worldwide already use. This lowers the barrier to entry and compresses code, saving on-chain storage.

3. It is designed with future scalability in mind. Most trending ZK technologies are adopting RISC-V as the standard. Rialo is pre-designed to easily absorb the latest ZK tech or other VMs later on. They are thinking several moves ahead.

4. WASM lacks a native gas model, EVM is outdated, and eBPF is tricky to manage. While others are busy patching legacy issues, Rialo chose RISC-V to build the fastest, safest, and most predictable blockchain from the ground up.

Why Rialo Uses RISC-V Underneath

At the core of any execution environment is its Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) the fundamental boundary between software and hardware that defines how a computer executes instructions. Rather than building on top of high-level or specialized bytecode, @RialoHQ  believes that a blockchain's performance and security depend on a robust, standardized ISA foundation.

Rialo has chosen RISC-V, specifically the RV64EMC variant, as its core execution environment. After careful evaluation, Rialo decided not to use WASM, eBPF, EVM, and Move VM.

The reasons for selecting RISC-V (RV64EMC):
1. Single-pass compilation is a feature, not an optimization Rialo leverages RISC-V’s design to perform single-pass compilation. This ensures that the translation from bytecode to machine code is fast, predictable, and simple, significantly reducing the attack surface for compiler exploits compared to multi-pass systems.

2. A real ISA buys you a real toolchain By using a standard CPU ISA, Rialo gains immediate access to mature, industry-standard toolchains like LLVM, GCC, and Rust. This allows developers to use professional-grade debuggers and profilers that have been refined over decades.

3. Open standard, lower long-term risk RISC-V is a community-driven open standard. This neutrality protects Rialo from the risks associated with proprietary VMs or those controlled by a single entity, ensuring the platform's longevity and broad ecosystem support.

4. Smaller programs matter (compressed instructions) The "C" extension in RV64EMC enables compressed instructions, which reduces the binary size of smart contracts. This efficiency leads to lower storage costs, faster network propagation, and improved cache performance.

5. Developer experience is not optional RISC-V allows developers to write in high-level languages they already know, such as Rust or C++, without needing to learn obscure, blockchain-specific virtual machine languages. This lowers the barrier to entry and reduces coding errors.

6. Determinism and metering come from canonicalization The simplicity of the RISC-V instruction set ensures strict determinism across all nodes. It enables precise, instruction-level gas metering, which is essential for maintaining consensus and preventing "out-of-gas" or infinite loop vulnerabilities.

7. Defense-in-depth sandboxing RISC-V’s architecture supports robust isolation. Rialo utilizes this to create a secure sandbox that prevents smart contracts from accessing sensitive host resources, providing a layered security model that is more resilient than traditional JIT-based VMs.

8. Crypto agility, ZK readiness, and formal verification The mathematical clarity of RISC-V makes it ideal for Zero-Knowledge (ZK) proof generation and formal verification. Its modular nature also allows Rialo to adapt quickly to new cryptographic standards (Crypto Agility) as they emerge.

9. A formal ISA specification RISC-V is defined by a rigorous formal specification, providing a mathematically precise definition of how every instruction must behave. This eliminates ambiguity in execution and serves as a solid foundation for building secure and verifiable blockchain state transitions.

① User → Block N (온체인 시작)
유저가 트랜잭션을 발생시키면 Block N에서 컨트랙트가 실행됩니다. 여기서 중요한 포인트가 있습니다.

----------------------------------------
② Block N → Off-chain (비동기 실행)
이후 트랜잭션은 오프체인으로 이동합니다. 이미지 중앙의 초록색 박스가 이 구간이며 여기서 Rialo의 핵심 기술이 드러납니다.

이 과정은 Web2 개발자에게 익숙한 async / await 구조와 거의 동일합니다.
----------------------------------------

• 새로운 트랜잭션을 다시 만드는 게 아님
• Block N에서 멈췄던 실행을 그대로 이어서 재개

“온체인 실행 → 오프체인 대기 → 온체인 재개”가
하나의 연속된 트랜잭션처럼 동작합니다.

결과는 Block N+M에서 처리됩니다.

• callback 실행
• 결과 역시 암호화 상태 유지

Day 1 Monday January 5 -

Event Driven Execution
Reactivity with sub second on chain responses :

Rialo’s privacy and performance begin with execution itself.

Most chains rely on polling, bots, and external automation to react to real world events.
This is slow, brittle, and leaks intent through mempools and off chain infrastructure.

Rialo replaces this entirely with native event driven execution.

At an advanced level, the model works like this.

• Smart contracts can sleep, loop, and await events using async await and resumable execution
• Execution pauses deterministically across blocks instead of terminating
• Real world events such as API callbacks or data updates automatically resume execution
• Multiple concurrent proposers parallelize block production to preserve sub second latency

This mirrors Web2 asynchronous systems while remaining fully deterministic and verifiable.

Privacy is preserved even during reactive flows.

Sensitive event inputs can be encrypted before triggering execution so no plaintext data appears in mempools, logs, or intermediate state.

Key advantages :

• Eliminates polling, off chain bots, and oracle races
• Prevents strategy leakage during reactive execution
• Enables always on applications without monitoring infrastructure
Tradeoffs exist.
Long lived execution introduces additional state management complexity.
Rialo mitigates this through its supermodular architecture that tightly integrates execution and storage for atomic resumptions.

The real world impact is immediate.
• Private lending protocols reacting to credit events
• Agent systems responding to live market signals
• Applications pulling Web2 data without exposing intent or inputs
This is Web2 responsiveness running on decentralized infrastructure without sacrificing privacy.

📋Why Rialo Chose RISC-V for Smart Contract Execution
Smart contract execution is as critical to a blockchain as consensus itself.
Validators must execute untrusted code while operating under strict resource limits, and still arrive at identical results every time.
This requirement goes beyond choosing a virtual machine.
In practice, the fundamental properties of execution are determined at the instruction set architecture (ISA) level.

Determinism, gas metering, compiler predictability, performance characteristics, tooling, and security models are all downstream of this choice.
After evaluating WebAssembly (WASM), eBPF, and RISC-V, Rialo selected RISC-V, specifically the RV64EMC profile, as its smart contract execution target.

What a Blockchain Requires from an ISA
A blockchain execution environment must satisfy several non-negotiable requirements.

▫️Predictable compilation
Compilation time must be bounded. The compilation process itself must not become a denial-of-service vector.
▫️Determinism
The same input must always produce the same state transition, regardless of hardware or runtime environment.
▫️Native gas metering
Out-of-gas conditions must be enforceable with low overhead and precise control over execution termination.
▫️Strong sandboxing
The system must be designed under the assumption that adversarial code will be executed, without allowing failures to propagate to the host.
▫️Practical tooling
Debugging, profiling, and security auditing must be realistically achievable using established developer tools.
If even one of these properties is missing, ad hoc mechanisms accumulate, the system grows more complex, and the attack surface expands.

Why RISC-V, and Why RV64EMC
One of the key reasons Rialo chose RISC-V is that it enables single-pass static recompilation/translation.
This is not merely a performance optimization. It is closer to a security property, because it prevents compilation time itself from becoming an attack surface.

The RV64E profile limits the register file to 16 registers, with 15 usable general-purpose registers.
This aligns closely with the 15 usable general-purpose registers available on x86-64.
As a result, minimal spilling and code generation becomes more predictable. This helps avoid pathological compilation paths and lowers the risk of attacks that exploit excessive or unbounded compilation behavior.

RISC-V also provides several practical advantages:
▫️Mature standard toolchains including LLVM, GCC, and Rust
▫️An open ISA standard, reducing long-term ecosystem and vendor risk
▫️Direct reuse of existing CPU debugging and analysis tools such as gdb, lldb, and DWARF
▫️Reduced code size through the compressed instruction (C) extension, which is particularly valuable in onchain execution environments

Determinism and Gas Metering via Canonicalization
Rialo does not execute RISC-V ELF binaries directly in consensus.
ELF is not a canonical artifact suitable for consensus execution. Compiler, linker, and layout differences can affect section ordering, metadata, alignment, and padding while preserving semantics.

Instead, Rialo introduces a canonicalization step that converts ELF into a deterministic bytecode representation designed for consensus execution.

During this step, execution is validated and constraints required for determinism and enforceable resource usage are defined before any code runs.

As a result, when execution begins, all relevant rules and limits are already fixed, and sources of nondeterminism are removed at the consensus layer.

Security Model and Long-Term Extensibility
Rialo’s RISC-V execution environment follows a defense-in-depth approach.
▫️Execution is isolated at the process level
▫️OS-level security mechanisms such as seccomp are employed
▫️Small code size and minimal dependencies reduce the overall attack surface

This design explicitly assumes the presence of malicious smart contracts.

From a long-term perspective, a RISC-V-based architecture also provides structural flexibility.
▫️New cryptographic primitives can be introduced at the library level without modifying the VM itself
▫️Architectural alignment with RISC-V-based zkVMs such as SP1 and RISC Zero
▫️The ability, in principle, to host other execution environments such as the EVM or Move VM as guest systems if required

How Do the Boundaries Between Web2 and Web3 Narrow?

Rialo’s Native Web Connectivity Strategy

In the blockchain industry, the term “Web2–Web3 bridge” is no longer unfamiliar.
In most cases, however, it still refers to indirect integration architectures built on oracles, external servers, and dedicated middleware layers.

While these approaches enable fast integration, they also introduce additional trust assumptions and structural complexity.

Rialo starts from a different question:

“Why must Web2 connectivity always be handled outside the chain?”

This line of inquiry leads to what Rialo calls Native Web Connectivity.

Reinterpreting the Web2–Web3 Bridge

Reducing the Connection Layer

Traditional Web2 integration in blockchains typically follows this pattern:

Web2 services → oracles or servers → smart contracts

Increased trust assumptions

Expanded security boundaries

Higher architectural complexity

Rialo does not attempt to replicate this structure as-is.
Instead, its goal is to absorb as much of the integration layer as possible into the platform itself.

The key distinction is important:
Rialo is not claiming to fully onchain all Web2 interactions.
Rather, it aims to structurally reduce reliance on external middleware.
This approach is enabled by two architectural choices:
A RISC-V–based general-purpose execution environment
Compatibility with the Solana Virtual Machine (SVM)

Together, these allow Rialo to avoid lock-in to a single VM while maintaining continuity with the existing Solana ecosystem—its tooling, languages, and development patterns.
As a result, Web2 integration is designed to be closely coupled with the chain’s execution environment, rather than pushed into a separate backend stack.

The Meaning of Email and Social Login Integration

Lowering UX Friction Without Shifting Trust
Email and social logins have long been controversial in Web3.
They are convenient, but often viewed as compromises that weaken decentralization or security assumptions.

Rialo approaches this tension through clear role separation:

Authentication uses Web2-friendly mechanisms
Account state and permissions are governed by onchain rules

Asset movement and contract execution remain controlled by chain logic

In this model, email or social accounts act as onboarding interfaces, not as replacements for the system’s trust model.

Crucially, this does not mean that private keys are “eliminated.”
Rialo’s focus is on reducing key exposure to users and improving UX, while leaving the ultimate security guarantees anchored in the chain’s execution rules.

This structure delivers practical benefits:

Lower onboarding friction for new users

Reduced UX burden for developers managing keys and accounts
User flows that more closely resemble familiar Web2 services

The Shift in Developer Experience

Making Web3 Feel Less “Special”

The most immediate impact of Rialo’s Web2 integration strategy is felt in developer experience (DX).
Developers can:

Reuse familiar Web API patterns and event-driven designs

Reduce the need for complex external servers or bridge infrastructure
Define clearer boundaries between frontend logic and onchain execution

This goes beyond simple convenience.
As architecture becomes simpler:

The scope of security audits narrows
The number of potential failure points decreases
Time-to-market improves

For many Web2 developers, the biggest barrier to entering Web3 is not the concepts themselves, but the excessive structural complexity surrounding them.
Rialo’s design choices explicitly aim to reduce that burden.

The Practical Question Rialo Is Asking

Rialo’s Web2–Web3 strategy is not centered on TPS races or fee optimization.
Instead, it focuses on a more fundamental question:

“If blockchains are to become real execution environments for applications,
how much of the surrounding system should be considered part of the chain’s design scope?”

Email authentication, social login, and natural integration with web services have long been treated as offchain concerns.

Rialo does not attempt full onchain purity.
Instead, it explores a pragmatic middle ground: tighter structural integration and reduced dependency surfaces.
If this approach matures, future dApps may no longer feel like blockchain applications at all.
They may simply feel like well-built internet services—
familiar to users, approachable for developers, and quietly powered by a blockchain underneath.

Why parallel execution fails without the right assumptions

Parallel execution is often presented as a simple upgrade:
more cores, more speed, higher throughput.
But in blockchains, parallelism is not a free win.
It only works if the system makes the right assumptions about conflict.

Every execution model starts with a belief:
Conflicts are common

or Conflicts are rare

That belief quietly governs everything that follows.

If a system assumes conflicts are common,
it will prioritize safety before execution.
Transactions wait. Access is restricted.
Results are predictable — but parallelism shrinks quickly.

If a system assumes conflicts are rare,
it will prioritize speed first.
Everything runs immediately.
But the cost shows up later as retries, wasted computation, and inconsistent UX under load.

Neither assumption is universally correct.
The mistake is treating concurrency control as a single choice,
instead of a design parameter tied to workload reality.
Read-heavy systems behave very differently from write-heavy ones.
Low-contention environments reward optimism.
High-contention environments demand control.
This is why performance is not defined by TPS,
but by how execution degrades when assumptions break.

Rialo approaches parallel execution from this angle:
not asking “how fast can we go,”
but “what happens when the system is wrong about conflicts?”
Correctness under stress matters more than speed at idle.
Predictability matters more than peak benchmarks.
Parallel execution is not about doing more at once.
It’s about deciding when not to.
That decision is where real blockchain performance is designed.

How Does Concurrency Control Govern Parallel Execution: Two Execution Strategies Compared by @RialoHQ ⚙️ [@itachee_x ]

Rialo focuses on a core question when introducing parallel execution: when and how conflicts are handled fundamentally shapes the execution model📌 

In a parallel execution environment, multiple transactions run at the same time. so the moment they touch the same state, conflicts can occur ⚠️

➜ How these conflicts are controlled directly determines parallelism, performance, and user experience.

There are two primary approaches to addressing this problem: Pessimistic Execution and Optimistic Execution.

Both approaches guarantee serializability, ensuring that the result of parallel execution is equivalent to some sequential order.

However, they differ in when conflicts are handled and where the associated costs are paid 💰

Pessimistic Execution: Preventing Conflicts in Advance 🛑

Pessimistic execution assumes that conflicts are likely to occur.

Before execution, transactions declare which states they intend to read and write (read/write sets).

and the system uses this information to assess potential conflicts between transactions.

If two transactions may access the same state, some of them are prevented from executing and moved into a waiting state ⏸️

Only transactions that are guaranteed not to conflict are allowed to run in parallel.

The system processes transactions in conflict-free batches groups of transactions that can safely execute together.

The main advantage of this approach is stability:
• Execution results are never invalidated
• Transactions do not need to be rolled back or re-executed
• Behavior is predictable and easy to reason about ✅

However, this stability comes at the cost of parallelism, due to a mechanism known as Exclusive Access.

What Is Exclusive Access? 🔒

Exclusive Access is a policy where a transaction prevents other transactions from accessing the same state while it is executing.

A key point is that many pessimistic models do not finely distinguish between reads and writes.

➜ As a result, even if a transaction is only reading the state of a specific account, other transactions may be blocked from accessing that account at all even for reads.

This leads to false sharing: situations where simple, non-conflicting read-only operations are forced to wait, despite not causing real conflicts 👀

Rialo identifies this as the most critical limitation of pessimistic execution.

The Structural Limit of Pessimistic Execution 📉

In summary, pessimistic execution behaves as follows:

Even a small possibility of conflict can halt transaction execution

• Parallelism collapses quickly due to exclusive access
• Read-heavy workloads suffer significant performance degradation

As a result, the benefits of parallel execution rapidly disappear, and execution flow converges back toward near-sequential processing.

At this point, Rialo poses a fundamental question:
 “Instead of preventing conflicts in advance, is it possible to design an execution model that assumes conflicts?”

👉 This question leads to another parallel execution model: Optimistic Execution.

[ A New Horizon in Blockchain Technology: Parallel Execution Architecture and Rialo’s Innovation ]

The history of blockchain technology has been a journey of adding the challenge of scalability onto a solid foundation of decentralization and security. Early models such as Bitcoin and Ethereum adopted a sequential execution method, where every transaction is processed one by one in a single line. While this structure guaranteed flawless verification, it carried a fatal bottleneck.

Much like thousands of vehicles trying to pass through a single-lane road, a single complex smart contract could obstruct the entire network’s flow. This technical constraint led to skyrocketing gas fees and processing delays, becoming the greatest obstacle to blockchain evolving into a mainstream financial infrastructure.

The solution that emerged to overcome this single-lane limitation is Parallel Execution Architecture. This approach applies the principle of multi-core processors, which are already a standard in modern computing, to the blockchain. By breaking down a massive workload into smaller tasks, the system enables transactions to be processed simultaneously. The core of parallel execution lies in separating independent transactions that use different data sets and processing them across multiple lanes at once.

Within this new framework, next-generation protocols like Rialo utilize a sophisticated signaling system known as concurrency control. Rialo maximizes network efficiency by combining two distinct methods. These include the following.

1. Optimistic Concurrency Control executes transactions first, based on the realistic assumption that most will not conflict, and verifies them later.
2. Pessimistic Concurrency Control coordinates data access in advance for critical segments, ensuring stability where it matters most.

Put simply, the system is designed to flow as fast as possible, intervening precisely only when a problem arises. 

Rialo takes this a step further by implementing a visualization dashboard for these complex internal mechanisms. This allows users to intuitively see data flowing in parallel, like a stream of stars in a galaxy. This is not mere technical showmanship, but an attempt to transform the inner workings of a blockchain into a visible order.

Rialo’s innovation does not stop at parallel execution. The protocol redefines the blockchain not as an isolated island, but as a Reactive Backend directly connected to the internet. While traditional chains relied on expensive oracle systems to access external data, Rialo’s smart contracts are designed to react directly to external events. By adding Deterministic Wrapping technology, which converts uncertain external inputs into certain blockchain states, Rialo ensures rock-solid stability.

These structural changes translate directly into economic fairness. Rialo’s Gas Calculation Mechanism does not determine costs based solely on computational volume. Instead, it factors in how much a specific transaction obstructs the parallel flow of others. Consequently, users who perform parallel-friendly transactions can utilize the network at a significantly lower cost.

Ultimately, the high-pass nature of parallel execution transcends pure technical achievement to transform the entire user experience. We are entering the era of Invisible Crypto, where users log in with emails or phone numbers instead of complex wallet addresses and seed phrases, and enjoy real-time payments without worrying about gas fees.

A future where real-world assets such as real estate and bonds are liquidated in real time, and insurance claims are automatically paid out the moment an accident occurs, is no longer a distant dream. 

On the multi-lane highway paved by pioneering protocols like Rialo, blockchain is evolving beyond a specialized technology into a universal infrastructure that sustains our daily lives.

turns into ambiguity.

Why @RialoHQ Redesigns the Execution Model from the Ground Up (feat. Parallel Execution) ⚙️💡 @itachee_x 

In modern computing environments, the key driver of performance improvement is parallelism the ability to process multiple tasks at the same time.

To understand this, it helps to first look at the relationship between the CPU and its core components. 

 ➜ The CPU is the central processing unit responsible for managing computations and instructions across the system, and inside it are multiple cores that perform the actual calculations 🧠

Modern servers and cloud infrastructures are able to process massive amounts of data at high speed precisely because these many cores can execute different tasks simultaneously.

However, the execution model of traditional blockchains has structural limitations that prevent them from fully utilizing this hardware capability.

On most blockchains, transactions must be processed one by one in the order they arrive. 

Even when running on high-performance CPUs with many cores, the rules of the execution model allow only a single transaction to be processed at a time. 

➜ As a result, most cores remain idle, and only a small fraction of the available computational power is actually used.

In other words, while modern computing has evolved toward a model where many workers operate in parallel, traditional blockchains remain stuck in a system where tasks are handled one at a time. As user demand grows and transaction volume surges, queues grow longer, execution slows down, and fees rise creating unavoidable bottlenecks.

This is exactly the point where Rialo begins its inquiry 🔍

Rialo does not start from the goal of simply making blockchains slightly faster. Instead, it begins with the premise that scalability cannot be structurally solved unless the execution model itself is redesigned with modern hardware in mind.

Based on this understanding, Rialo presents parallel execution as a core assumption for addressing scalability ☑️

Parallel execution aims to increase blockchain throughput by executing multiple transactions simultaneously and fully leveraging available computational resources. 

However, in a blockchain setting, parallel execution is not merely about processing transactions simultaneously. It must also guarantee serializability the property that parallel execution yields the same outcome as a valid sequential execution order.

Rialo treats this condition as a non-negotiable starting point when designing its parallel execution model. 

📌If this guarantee is violated, parallel execution does not lead to better performance, it leads to asset inconsistencies and errors.

Consider a simple example 🧐 

Suppose an account has a balance of 100 ETH. 
Transaction A subtracts 30 ETH, and Transaction B adds 50 ETH. 

Under sequential execution, whether A ➜ B, B ➜ A is always 120 ETH.

However, under parallel execution, both transactions may read the same initial state 100 ETH at the same time, complete their calculations, and then write their results back. 

Depending on the order in which those writes occur, the final balance may end up as 70 ETH or 150 ETH⚠️

This situation, where multiple transactions access the same state and produce different outcomes depending on execution timing is known as a conflict.

The very first challenge Rialo confronted when designing parallel execution was how to control these conflicts while preserving parallelism. 

Two representative approaches to solving this problem are pessimistic execution and optimistic execution▶️

블록체인 실행 환경이 병렬로 전환된 지금, 상태와 읽기, 쓰기 구조를 이해하는 일은 단순한 기술적 지식을 넘어 네트워크 성능과 비용 효율성을 결정짓는 핵심이다. Rialo는 이 구조를 시각화하고 최적화함으로써 트랜잭션 병렬성의 효율을 극대화하는 병렬 블록체인이다.

모든 연산은 데이터를 읽고, 처리하고, 다시 쓰는 흐름을 따른다. 순차적 실행에서는 문제가 없지만, 병렬 환경에서는 여러 트랜잭션이 동시에 같은 상태에 접근할 때 충돌이 발생한다. 이를 상태 경합이라 부르며, 잘못 처리하면 데이터 유실로 이어질 수 있다.

Rialo는 이를 해결하기 위해 두 가지 병렬 실행 전략을 제공한다. 첫 번째는 결정론적 병렬화다. 트랜잭션이 어떤 상태를 읽고 쓸지를 사전에 선언하고, 충돌 가능성이 없는 트랜잭션만 병렬로 배치하여 실행한다. 이 방식은 재실행이 없고 안정적인 처리 속도를 제공한다. 두 번째는 낙관적 병렬화다. 트랜잭션을 일단 동시에 실행한 뒤, 쓰기 직전에 상태 값의 변화를 확인한다. 충돌이 감지되면 해당 트랜잭션만 롤백 후 재실행한다. 이 방식은 복잡한 연산이나 외부 데이터가 개입되는 상황에 유리하다.

Rialo의 병렬 구조는 단지 속도 개선에 그치지 않는다. 첫째, 충돌이 적을수록 가스비가 줄고, 실행 속도가 빨라진다. 둘째, 상태를 독립적으로 분리하는 설계는 트랜잭션 간 경합을 최소화해 전체 처리량을 끌어올린다. 셋째, Rialo는 RISC-V 아키텍처 기반으로 구성되어 병렬 하드웨어의 성능을 극대화한다. 마지막으로 Rialo는 외부 API 데이터와의 실시간 상호작용에서 높은 데이터 무결성과 응답성을 유지할 수 있다.

리알로(@RialoHQ)는 단순히 더 빠른 레이어1이나 새로운 체인이 아닙니다. 리알로는 지금의 웹3가 왜 여전히 실험 단계에 머물러 있는가 라는 부분을 해결하려고 해요. 

현재 대부분의 블록체인은 외부 세계와 제대로 연결되지 못하고 있습니다. 실제 서비스에 필요한 API, 신원 정보, 결제 시스템, 기업 데이터는 모두 오프체인에 있는데, 퍼블릭 체인은 투명성이 기본값이라 민감한 데이터를 다룰 수 없기 때문이에요. 그래서 오라클, 봇, 인덱서, RPC, 릴레이어 같은 미들웨어가 덕지덕지 붙고, 이 중 하나만 멈춰도 앱과 자동화가 그대로 멈춰버리죠. 이것이 웹3의 ‘숨겨진 운영 비용’입니다.

리알로는 이 구조를 뒤집습니다. 핵심은 온체인에서 시작한 로직이, 오프체인 작업을 안전하게 수행한 뒤 다시 온체인으로 자연스럽게 이어지는 비동기 트랜잭션(Async + Continuation)입니다. 

트랜잭션은 한 블록 안에서 모든 걸 끝낼 필요가 없어요. 먼저 암호화된 요청을 온체인에서 만들고, 리알로의 프라이빗 실행 환경(TEE, MPC 등)에서 외부 API나 실제 데이터를 처리한 뒤, 결과가 나오면 그 시점에서 트랜잭션을 다시 이어서 실행해요. 

이 과정에서 데이터는 노출되지 않고, 결과는 검증 가능하게 돌아온다. 웹2 개발자가 async/await를 쓰듯, 리알로에서는 이 흐름이 프로토콜 레벨에서 기본 동작이죠.

여기에 프라이버시가 옵션이 아니라 기본값이라는 점이 리알로의 결정적 차별점이에요! 리알로는 '모두 공개'와 '완전 비공개' 중 하나를 강요하지 않아요. 

필요한 정보만 선택적으로 증명하고, 나머지는 숨길 수 있는 조건부 프라이버시를 전제로 설계됐어요. 이 구조 덕분에 신용 점수, 사용자 인증, 기업 API 키처럼 기존 블록체인에서는 다룰 수 없던 영역이 온체인 로직 안으로 들어올 수 있게 되었습니다. Jan Camenisch가 합류한 이유도 여기에 있구요. 리알로는 단순한 체인이 아니라, 프라이버시와 검증 가능한 연산을 실제로 운영 가능한 수준으로 묶는 오케스트레이션 레이어를 만들고 있죠.

마지막으로 리알로의 경제 구조는 앱이 계속 살아있게 만듭니다. Stake-for-Service(SfS)를 통해 스테이킹 수익은 지갑에 쌓이는 게 아니라, 가스, 스토리지, 자동 실행 비용을 자동으로 지불하는 흐름이 되어요. 덕분에 앱은 잔고를 계속 관리할 필요 없이 장기간 안정적으로 운영될 수 있고, 개발자는 봇과 미들웨어를 유지하는 대신 로직에만 집중할 수 있죠. 

리알로가 말하는 비전은 분명합니다. 현실 세계와 온체인을 가르는 벽을 허물고, 프라이버시, 자동화, 지속 가능성을 기본값으로 갖는 ‘진짜 돌아가는 웹3 앱’을 만드는 것이에요!

Why Privacy Fails in Crypto – And How Rialo SfS Fixes It

Privacy in crypto is widely misunderstood. Most solutions focus on hiding wallet identities, but on-chain research reveals the real leaks come from funding patterns and service usage.

1. Where Privacy Actually Breaks
Even with privacy wallets or mixers:
- KYC on-ramps tie real-world identities to funds.
- Repeated wallet top-ups create traceable patterns.
- Gas, storage, and execution fees expose timing and behavioral metadata.
- Middleware (RPCs, indexers, schedulers) quietly log everything.

Result: Privacy tools mask the user, but the infrastructure still watches them.

2. The Core Problem: The Endless Funding Chain
Every interaction requires:
- New gas payments.
- New service payments.
- New links between capital and activity.

This creates a funding trail, a persistent chain connecting identity, capital, and behavior over time. As long as users must keep paying to stay active, privacy remains fragile.

3. Rialo SfS: A Structural Revolution
Rialo’s Stake-for-Service (SfS) model introduces a new primitive:
- Stake $RLO once.
- The stake automatically generates service credits.
- Services consume credits, no direct token transfers.
- No visible link between usage and capital movement.

4. The Biggest Breakthrough: Breaking the Funding Chain
Rialo doesn’t just hide transactions, it eliminates the need to fund them.
- No recurring top-ups → No periodic identity signals.
- No direct gas payments → No behavioral leakage.
- Activity runs in a closed loop backed by stake.

Privacy becomes infrastructural, not optional.

5. Why This Matters Long-Term
SfS shifts privacy from:
- Event-based & temporary → Systemic & perpetual.
- User-managed → Protocol-enforced.

Users no longer “prove” their identity through every payment.

Rialo: A Next-Generation Blockchain Designed for Real-World Integration

Rialo is not positioning itself as “just another Layer 1.”
Rather than competing on raw performance metrics like speed or transaction fees, the project starts from a different question: can a blockchain meaningfully integrate with real-world services?

In this sense, Rialo’s core challenge is not Web3 performance optimization, but how Web2 and Web3 can be structurally connected within a single execution environment.

A Blockchain Built for Web2-Level Experience

Rialo is a blockchain network under development by Subzero Labs.
According to its official documentation, the project’s primary goal is to bring Web2-level developer experience and user experience into Web3.

This reflects a clear design philosophy: instead of treating blockchain as a specialized, isolated system, Rialo aims to make it a runtime that can blend naturally with existing web services and infrastructure.

Architectural Choices and Technical Direction

From a technical standpoint, Rialo outlines several distinct design decisions:
A RISC-V–based execution environment for smart contracts and on-chain logic

Directional compatibility with the Solana VM (eBPF), enabling partial reuse of tooling and developer experience from the Solana ecosystem

An architecture that allows direct interaction between smart contracts and web data or APIs

These elements are consistently described across Rialo’s official website and technical blog posts, forming the backbone of its proposed execution model.

A Different Question Than Traditional L1s

This approach stands apart from the dominant Layer 1 narrative, which has largely focused on TPS, fees, and scalability.
Rialo’s underlying question is more fundamental:
Can a blockchain move beyond token transfers and financial primitives to become part of real service logic itself?
Its architectural choices can be seen as one possible design-level answer to that question.

Privacy as a Structural Requirement

Another notable aspect of Rialo’s design is that privacy is treated as a foundational element, not an optional add-on.

When a blockchain is intended to interact directly with real-world data and web infrastructure, privacy becomes a structural necessity rather than a feature toggle. Rialo explicitly frames privacy in this way within its public materials, positioning it as a core design constraint.

Project Background and Funding

Some elements of Rialo’s background are already confirmed.
Subzero Labs has reportedly raised approximately $20 million in seed funding, with participation from Pantera Capital, Coinbase Ventures, and Hashed, among others.
While the project remains at an early stage, this level of backing suggests that its technical direction and problem framing have gained credibility within the crypto investment landscape.

Important Fact Check

There are also clear limitations on what is publicly known:

❌ No official Testnet or Mainnet launch dates have been announced

❌ No details on token economics or exchange listings have been disclosed

At this stage, most publicly available information focuses on vision, architecture, and design principles, rather than live network performance or adoption metrics.

Rialo’s Position in the L1 Landscape

Taken together, Rialo should be viewed not as a finished network, but as an early-stage Layer 1 project designing a new execution paradigm for real-world integration.

From a fact-based perspective within the L1 competitive landscape:

Strength: a fundamentally different problem definition centered on real-world services and UX
Uncertainty: network effects, adoption, and real usage remain unproven

This is not an evaluation, but an accurate description of Rialo’s current stage.

What Actually Matters Going Forward

Ultimately, the key question for Rialo is not when it launches.

The real points to watch are:
Can this architecture be implemented as a functioning network?

Can Web2 ↔ Web3 integration operate reliably in practice?

For now, Rialo is in the phase of revealing structure and direction, not proving outcomes.
Its future Testnet releases and early technical implementations will serve as the first concrete validation of whether this vision can translate into a working, real-world blockchain system.

So Where Does Rialo Actually Place Responsibility?

Designing responsibility is meaningless unless it answers one concrete question:
Where does responsibility live when something goes wrong?

This is where abstract discussions end and structure begins.
------------------------------------------------------------
In many Web3 systems, responsibility is everywhere — and nowhere.

Execution is decentralized.

Governance is collective.

Incentives are distributed.

But when failure occurs:
- no single layer owns the outcome
- costs are externalized
- accountability dissolves into process

Responsibility without an address is symbolic, not functional.
------------------------------------------------------------
Most protocols avoid placing responsibility at the core.

Why?
Because responsibility introduces constraints.
Once responsibility is anchored:
- some actions must be rejected
- some behaviors must be limited
- some outcomes must be explicitly handled

So instead, responsibility is often pushed to the edges:
- users
- governance forums
- “the community”

This preserves flexibility —
but sacrifices clarity.
------------------------------------------------------------
@RialoHQ's design direction suggests a different choice.

Instead of treating responsibility as an emergent property, @RialoHQ attempts ts locate it within a defined structural layer.

Not everywhere.

Not nowhere.

But somewhere specific enough to:
- observe outcomes
- recognize failure
- and enforce boundaries

This doesn’t mean Rialo controls everything.

It means the system acknowledges:
some responsibilities cannot be outsourced to incentives alone.
----------------------------------------------------------
Placing responsibility introduces trade-offs.

It enables:
- clearer failure attribution
- measurable system behavior
- bounded expectations

But it also forbids:
- infinite composability
- ambiguity-driven growth
- responsibility-free experimentation

This is not a neutral choice.
It’s a commitment.
------------------------------------------------------------

Why TPS is not the core of blockchain performance

When people talk about blockchain performance,

The real question isn’t
how many transactions you process,
but how correctly you process them.

In modern blockchains, parallel execution is unavoidable.
The bottleneck is no longer speed —
it’s conflict management.

When multiple transactions touch the same state at the same time,
the system must decide:
•who waits
•who retries
•and how correctness is preserved

If this isn’t handled properly,
higher TPS simply means more retries, more failures, and worse UX.

That’s why the real performance lever is not TPS,

Optimistic and pessimistic execution are not about “which is better.”

Low contention favors optimism.
High contention demands control.

Blockchain performance is not a benchmark.

What Is FHE, and How Does @RialoHQ View It? 🔐

To make privacy a default property, Rialo adopts a Hybrid Toolbox approach, selecting the most appropriate cryptographic technique based on the purpose of each computation 🧰

As discussed earlier, MPC distributes secrets across multiple participants and performs computation collaboratively.

While this preserves the confidentiality of inputs, it comes with a limitation: the computation process itself is not fully maintained in an encrypted state, and the final result must be reconstructed through a predefined recovery process ⚠️

 ➜ To address this limitation, Rialo introduces FHE (Fully Homomorphic Encryption) 🔒

FHE allows computation to be performed directly on encrypted data.

Data is encrypted once and never decrypted during computation. The result remains encrypted as well, and only an entity with the appropriate authorization can decrypt the final output 🔑

From a theoretical standpoint, FHE represents the most complete solution for privacy:
• The executor learns nothing about the input 
• All intermediate states remain encrypted
• Only the final result is selectively revealed

Because computation happens without revealing anything at all, FHE appears to represent the pinnacle of privacy 🛡️

However, this level of privacy comes at a cost.

Computation on encrypted data is significantly more expensive and slower than standard execution.

As operations accumulate, ciphertext noise increases, requiring periodic ciphertext maintenance, which further adds to computational overhead 🐢

For this reason, Rialo does not force the use of slow FHE for all computations. Instead, FHE is treated as a specialized tool, applied only where it makes the most sense 🎯

• When handling extremely sensitive data
• When privacy is more critical than execution speed
• When analyzing long-term stored data 
where real-time performance is not required

In summary, while FHE is the most ideal privacy-preserving technology in theory, it is not always the most practical choice ⚖️

Therefore, rather than relying on FHE alone, Rialo combines MPC, TEE, and ZK leveraging the strengths of each technique while compensating for their respective limitations 🧡 @itachee_x

Why Most dApps Are Over-Engineered by Default

The Problem Rialo Starts From

Most dApps are not complex by choice.

They are complex by necessity.

This necessity exists because most blockchains are still passive ledgers.
This is the core assumption Rialo challenges.

The Illusion of Simple Smart Contracts

On paper, smart contracts look clean.

Deterministic logic
Immutable state
Clear inputs and outputs

In practice, that simplicity disappears the moment
an application touches the real world.

A single feature turns into:

A contract
An oracle
An off-chain service
A bot to trigger execution
A dashboard to monitor failures

The contract remains simple.

The system does not.
From Rialo’s perspective, this is not poor engineering.
It is a predictable outcome of ledger-based execution.

Glue Code Is the Real dApp

Most production dApps today are not truly on-chain.
They are:
Distributed systems held together by scripts
Cron jobs pretending to be decentralization
Human operators standing behind emergency switches

The blockchain is only one component.
The glue is everything else.
This is the layer Rialo aims to eliminate,
not by better tooling, but by changing the execution model itself.

Why Developers Keep Rebuilding the Same Scaffolding

Every team ends up implementing the same patterns.

Watchers
Keepers
Retry logic
Reorg handling
Fallback paths

Not because they want to.

Because passive ledgers require someone to:
Observe
Decide
Trigger

Again and again.

Rialo frames this as a structural tax on developers.

Active Networks Remove the Scaffolding

When execution is condition-driven, as in Rialo’s model:

No one needs to wake up the contract
No external service needs to babysit state
Fewer failure modes exist by design
Logic lives where execution happens.
Not half on-chain and half somewhere else.

Less Code, More Guarantees

There is a paradox here.

Active networks often require less code
to deliver stronger guarantees.
Not because the system is simpler,
but because entire categories of glue disappear.

Less surface area.
Less trust.
Less to maintain.

This tradeoff is central to how Rialo positions itself.

What Developers Actually Want

Developers do not want:
More tools
More frameworks
More abstractions

They want:
Fewer moving parts
Fewer things that can break
Fewer alerts at 3 a.m.

Active networks do not make applications magical.

They make the system honest.

And that is the problem Rialo is trying to solve.

Diving deeper into privacy-preserving async transactions at @RialoHQ – one of the most exciting primitives emerging in blockchain for 2026.

As founder Ade recently highlighted, the big question is: How does a transaction suspend to handle offchain data securely, then resume onchain without ever exposing sensitive information?

The answer is native reactive transactions built on a continuation model. These allow transactions to pause for real-world inputs (e.g., API responses, timers, market prices, or personal data like credit scores) and resume seamlessly – all while maintaining end-to-end privacy and full onchain verifiability.

Here’s how it works:
1/ Onchain start: Tx initiates in Block N as an E2E-encrypted user request.

2/ Native pause: Execution suspends securely – encrypted request routes offchain, zero mempool leaks (no oracles needed).

3/ Private computation: Orchestrated via MPC, FHE, and TEEs – plaintext never exposed, even to operators; results verifiably attested.

4/ Encrypted return: Outcome attested and sent back securely.

5/ Seamless resume: Tx continues in Block N+M with full consensus intact.

This feels just like async/await in Web2 languages (Node.js, Python) – intuitive for traditional developers – but fully verifiable, compliant, and private on a Layer 1 blockchain.

No third-party oracles. No constant polling or fragile offchain bots. No “glue logic” middleware that introduces failure points.
Instead, Rialo delivers native reactive execution: smart contracts that pull live web data directly (HTTPS calls), trigger on events/timers, and react autonomously to real-world signals – all with privacy-by-design at the core.

With cryptography legend Jan Camenisch on board emphasizing end-to-end privacy flows, Rialo is positioned perfectly for institutional adoption: personalized DeFi using real credit data, compliant RWA tokenization, autonomous agents integrating Web2 APIs securely, and everyday payments tied to email/phone without identity leaks.

What Is MPC, and How Does @RialoHQ Use It? 🔐

As discussed in the previous section, ZK proofs are extremely powerful tools for proving that a computation was performed correctly ✅

However, ZK proofs are primarily focused on verification, rather than serving as a general-purpose execution model for sensitive inputs themselves.
➜ This is where MPC comes into play 💡

What Is MPC? 🤝

MPC is a cryptographic approach that enables secure computation over sensitive data among multiple parties that do not trust each other.

In an MPC setup, a single sensitive input is split into multiple pieces, often referred to as shares.

Each participant holds only a fragment of the data and performs computations based solely on that fragment 🧩

➜ No single participant can see the entire dataset
➜ The final result can only be produced through cooperation among participants 🤝

In other words, everyone participates in the computation, but no one ever sees the full data.
This breaks the traditional assumption that sensitive computations require trusting a specific party or execution environment.

Instead, MPC enables confidential collaborative computation without relying on a single trusted entity 🔐

As a result, MPC is commonly explored in domains where trust assumptions must be minimized such as inter-institution financial analysis or privacy-sensitive medical research.

The Trade-offs of MPC ⚖️

MPC achieves strong trust minimization, but it comes with inherent trade-offs.

MPC protocols require ongoing interaction and coordination between participants throughout the computation process.

As computational complexity increases, this communication overhead grows rapidly, leading to degraded performance and higher latency ⏳

In summary, MPC has the following characteristics:
• Highly suitable for collaborative computation and cross-organization data aggregation
• Eliminates the need for a single trusted party
• Performance degrades with complexity, making it less suitable for real-time responses or complex execution logic

How Rialo Uses MPC 🧠

Rialo fully embraces these trade-offs.

Rather than adopting MPC as the default execution model for all computations, Rialo selectively deploys MPC only in situations where trust elimination is most critical 🎯

Within Rialo’s architecture:
• MPC is used as the mechanism for confidential, collaborative computation 
• ZK proofs are used to attest that the computation followed predefined rules and can be verified by anyone 

This separation allows Rialo to achieve both privacy and verifiability, without forcing every computation into a single cryptographic model.

Privacy isn’t about using the strongest cryptography everywhere.

so, Rialo assigns the right privacy technology to each role and FHE represents the deepest layer of trust minimization.

[ Rialo: Building the Real World Computer ]

The history of blockchain is a story of redefining the computer. It began as a simple ledger and evolved into a world computer with Ethereum. However, we eventually hit a wall. Legacy systems proved too heavy for modern hardware, setting clear limits on what next generation networks could become.

Rialo chose the RISC-V architecture as a strategic move to break through that wall and evolve blockchain into a true high performance computer.

Think of the existing EVM as an ancient engine inside a modern supercar. While the devices we use every day operate in 64 bit environments, the EVM insists on a unique 256 bit structure. This mismatch wastes resources and drives gas costs higher.

RISC-V speaks the same language as the hardware we actually use. Its simple and regular instruction set makes computation faster, lighter, and significantly cheaper.

At the same time, the industry is shifting toward verifiable compute. Instead of every node rerunning every calculation, correctness is checked through a mathematical receipt. This was impractical in legacy execution environments, but RISC-V makes computation far easier to translate into math. Heavy work can be done locally, with only a small certificate submitted to the network.

Traditional blockchains move only when a transaction is submitted. Rialo changes this with an event driven architecture. When predefined conditions are met, the system executes logic autonomously without external calls. This brings the responsiveness of modern cloud functions into Web3 while reducing reliance on fragile middleware.

The developer experience shifts as well. Engineers are no longer confined to blockchain specific languages. They can use familiar tools like Rust and C++ to build financial systems, AI workloads, and real world applications just like general purpose software.

Rialo is moving beyond recording numbers. It is building a global, trusted computing platform where verifiable compute is law.

In this model, computation no longer asks for trust.
It asks for proof.
This is what it means to build a real world computer.

Rialo 1337 explained simply
How real world market data was streamed onchain in real time.

@RialoHQ recently ran an experiment called Project 1337.
The goal was simple but extremely hard to execute.
Stream real world stock market prices onchain in real time at traditional finance speed.

This matters because bringing Real World Assets onchain is the next major step for DeFi to go mainstream.

1. The core problem with RWAs onchain : 

RWAs like stocks commodities and currencies depend on accurate real time prices.
Blockchains cannot access external data on their own.

Today this is handled by oracles but current oracle systems struggle with two big issues

• Latency :
Real markets update in milliseconds but oracle updates are delayed and unpredictable
This causes stale prices and broken trading experiences

• Trust :
Many oracles rely on multisigs committees or reputation based systems.
This introduces trust assumptions and attack surfaces.

Because of this it is very hard to build high performance perps or RWA markets onchain.

2. What Rialo did differently : 

Rialo built a single integrated pipeline that handles data ingestion processing verification and onchain publishing together.

Instead of outsourcing pricing to third party middleware Rialo collapses everything into one verifiable system.

The result :

Sub second latency
Cryptographic guarantees
No reliance on social trust or committees
Lower cost and lower complexity for developers.

3. What Project 1337 actually demonstrated :

Rialo streamed 1,337 live stock tickers onchain in real time.

Every ticker represented a real world stock,
Every price update was recorded as an onchain state change
Updates happened roughly every 300 milliseconds.

This was effectively an onchain Bloomberg style terminal but fully backed by verified blockchain state.

4. How the architecture works :

The system has five main components

1. Data sources :
Live market data came from Massive via real time WebSocket feeds
Each update included symbol price and timestamp

2. Pre processing and verification
Instead of pushing raw noisy data Rialo processed it before publishing :

• Noise filtering to remove meaningless micro fluctuations
• Momentum calculation called alpha to measure trend direction and speed
• Buy and sell pressure calculation called bias
• Risk estimation using full data ranges not just medians

All processing was cryptographically attested so anyone can verify correctness.

3. Onchain logic 
Processed data feeds into smart contracts like a perps controller :

These contracts
• Update internal market state
• Adjust funding rates
• Keep synthetic prices aligned with real prices

The contract does not guess prices.
It reacts to verified real world data in a continuous feedback loop.

4. Frontend :

A live dashboard showing 1,337 tickers updating several times per second
Every visual change reflects an onchain update not an offchain simulation

5. Why this is important :

Project 1337 proved that blockchains can handle real time financial data at traditional market speeds.

This unlocks several major use cases

• Perpetual DEXs with real time funding and pricing.
• RWA tokens that update fast enough to be used as active collateral.
• Onchain risk management using real statistical methods.
• New financial products built on public alpha and bias data.

Most importantly it removes the need for expensive middleware and fragile oracle stacks.

6. The bigger picture :

Rialo 1337 was a test not a product launch.
But it showed that real time onchain finance is achievable today.

When data ingestion computation and verification are designed together
Onchain systems no longer need to be slower or weaker than TradFi.

They can match it.

Rialo is not restricted like the regular traditional L1 chains, it can move cross chain and even teleport between Web3 and web2 worlds.

What Does It Actually Mean to Design Responsibility?

So far, this series has asked why.

Why roles matter.
Why problem selection matters.
Why responsibility has been so hard to place in Web3.

Now the question shifts.

What does it actually mean to design responsibility — instead of assuming it will emerge?
----------------------------------------------------------
In Web3, responsibility is often discussed as a cultural ideal.

If participants act in good faith, if incentives are aligned,
if governance is decentralized —
responsibility should somehow appear.

But systems don’t work on intentions.

They work on structure.

Responsibility isn’t something that emerges.
It’s something that must be assigned, constrained, and enforced by design.

Without structure, responsibility diffuses.
And what diffuses cannot be relied on.
------------------------------------------------------------
In Web2, responsibility is straightforward.

It lives in:
- roles
- authority
- and clearly defined failure costs

When something breaks, there is a place to point.
This is efficient — and centralized.

Web3 removed that hierarchy.
But in many cases, it didn’t replace it with an alternative structure.

The result wasn’t freedom.
It was ambiguity.

- authority is distributed
- incentives are abstract
- failure has no clear owner

Responsibility didn’t disappear.
It just lost its address.
------------------------------------------------------------
Designing responsibility doesn’t mean re-introducing hierarchy.

It means answering hard structural questions upfront:
- Where does responsibility sit?
- How is failure recognized?
- Who absorbs the cost when things go wrong?

What cannot be done because responsibility must remain bounded?

These questions don’t come at the end of design.

They are the design.

Ignoring them makes systems flexible —
but fragile.
------------------------------------------------------------
This is where earlier choices start to matter.

A project that defines its role,
narrows its problem space,
and treats responsibility as a constraint isn’t being conservative.

It’s being explicit.

@RialoHQ doesn’t present responsibility as a moral expectation.
It treats it as a structural requirement.

What that structure looks like —
and whether it can hold under pressure —
is the real question.
------------------------------------------------------------
Up to this point, the series focused on why responsibility matters.

From here on, the focus shifts.

Not why responsibility is important —
but how it can be structured without centralization.

That’s where design begins.

Why Active Networks Break the Oracle Model

Rialo’s Perspective

Oracles were never meant to scale.

They were meant to patch a problem.

That problem exists because blockchains were designed as ledgers.
This is the starting point of how Rialo approaches the oracle model.

What Oracles Actually Do

An oracle does one thing.

It imports truth from the outside world
into a system that cannot observe it.

Prices.
Events.
Outcomes.
APIs.
This worked. Temporarily.

But every oracle introduces:
An external dependency
A trust surface
A timing gap
The chain remains blind.
It simply listens to a messenger.
This is not a failure of oracle design.
It is a consequence of ledger-based systems.

The Hidden Cost of Oracles

Once applications rely on oracles,
they also inherit everything around them.

Update frequency
Operator incentives
Off-chain uptime
Dispute mechanisms after the fact
Developers respond by adding complexity.
Multiple feeds
Fallback logic
Manual overrides
Emergency pauses

The application keeps running.
But the architecture slowly degrades.

From Rialo’s viewpoint,
this is not a tooling problem.
It is a structural one.

Why This Is a Ledger Problem

Oracles exist because ledgers are passive.

A ledger cannot:
Watch continuously
React autonomously
Validate external causality in real time

So the world is compressed into:
Discrete updates
Snapshot values
Approximate representations of reality
Reality does not behave in snapshots.
This mismatch is where most Web3 fragility begins.

What Changes in an Active Network

In an active network, as defined by Rialo:
Observation is part of execution
Conditions drive logic
State evolves as inputs evolve
You do not import reality.
You bind execution to it.
No price pushes.
No periodic updates.
No trusted messengers racing the clock.

Execution responds to the world as it changes.

This Does Not Remove Truth. It Reframes It.

The question is no longer:
Is this oracle honest?
It becomes:

Is this condition verifiable?

That distinction matters.

Verification is something networks can enforce.
Trust is something they can only assume.

This shift sits at the center of Rialo’s design philosophy.

The End of the Oracle Era, As We Know It

Oracles will not disappear overnight.

But in active networks:

They stop being the backbone
They become optional adapters
They are no longer the source of truth
The system no longer waits for reality to knock.
It is already listening.
