Privacy ≠ ZK Alone
A focused take on why real Web3 privacy needs more than one tool............

Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZK) are powerful  they proving the correctness without revealing data.
But building truly private systems isn’t just about proof. It’s about secure computation on sensitive data.

👉 Core idea: Private Web3 needs a full cryptographic stack, not a single primitive.

One Privacy Goal: Confidential Computation

To compute on data without exposing it, ZK must work with other tools:

🟣 FHE (Fully Homomorphic Encryption).
Compute directly on encrypted data. No decryption, no data leaks. Ideal for shared private state.

🟤 MPC (Multi-Party Computation).
Multiple parties compute together without revealing inputs. Essential for key management & coordination.

🟢 TEEs (Trusted Execution Environments).
Hardware-level secure enclaves for fast, confidential execution when performance matters.

🔴 ZK (Zero Knowledge Proofs).
Ensures verifiability proving the computation was done correctly, privately.

Why Integration Matters👇

Platforms like @RialoHQ focus on privacy by design, where these tools work together at the execution layer not as add-ons.

This enables:
• Secure processing of sensitive data.
• Verifiable private automation.
• Selective disclosure & compliance.
• Hybrid Web2/Web3 workflows.

Bottom line:
The private internet won’t be built with ZK alone.
It will be built with a full privacy spectrum  programmable, composable, and integrated.

Why Web3 kept missing the real world

For years, Web3 focused on one question:
How do we bring real-world data onchain?

But that was never the real problem.

The real issue was execution.

Blockchains are designed for deterministic execution.
Every node must compute the same result, in the same way.
That model was never meant to handle real-time events, unstable APIs, or external systems.

So Web3 adapted the only way it could.
It pushed logic offchain.
Servers, bots, oracles, middleware.

The chain became a place to record outcomes,
not a system that actually reacts.

This wasn’t a lack of cryptography.
It was a limitation of architecture.

Rialo doesn’t try to “connect” blockchains to the web.
It redesigns how execution works.

Smart contracts define conditions.
Execution happens inside protocol-native mechanisms.
Web calls, automation, and external triggers operate within chain rules, not outside of them.

What matters is no longer that data was fetched,
but where and how execution happened.

Web3 didn’t fail because it couldn’t see the real world.
It failed because it wasn’t built to respond to it.

Change execution,
and the connection changes with it.

Production onchain products almost always end up looking the same

You need a source of real-world data: prices, statuses, event outcomes. That usually means a separate oracle or a service that keeps updating it.

You need actions to fire on time or on specific events: close a market, satisfy a condition, send a payout. That's where bots and cron scripts show up.

You need to connect chains: move an asset, pass a message, sync state - so you inherit bridges, wrapped tokens, and extra risk.

You need to talk to users: confirmations, codes, reminders. That becomes another layer - email/SMS/push, plus its own auth.

And every layer means setup, maintenance, monitoring, and more places where things can break. The more real world your product touches, the more infrastructure you pile around the contract.

@RialoHQ addresses this with a real-world blockchain approach: a network where external data and events are built into the stack.

:::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::

A typical flow on Rialo:

➯ an external event happens (a payment, a price move, a status update)
➯ the contract makes a web call and pulls the fact directly over HTTPS
➯ logic executes in an event-driven way, without constant bot polling
➯ the result reaches the user natively: encrypted message to email/phone/device, 2FA, scheduled tx, social login

---

What this removes from a developer's life:

➱ bots that keep the system moving
➱ the endless race to keep data updated
➱ part of the cross-chain glue layer (bridges and wrappers)
➱ manual orchestration that grows as the product scales

---

Result: fewer points of failure, faster iteration, and an experience closer to modern software - even if the core is onchain.

Understanding Oracles in Blockchain made simple :

Most smart contracts today are powerful but blind.

On chains like Ethereum or Solana smart contracts cannot see the real world. They cannot know prices weather scores payments or API responses on their own. They only understand what exists on chain.

This limitation created the need for oracles.

1. What oracles do

An oracle is a bridge between the blockchain and the real world.

• It fetches off chain data like ETH USD prices sports results or weather
• It delivers that data on chain so smart contracts can act on it

Example
A DeFi lending protocol needs the ETH USD price to decide collateral ratios.
An oracle periodically pushes that price to the contract.

Without oracles most DeFi and real world apps would not work.

2. The oracle problem

Oracles solve a problem but also create new ones.

• Centralization risk since many rely on a small set of providers
• Delays and latency because data updates are not instant
• Security risks as oracle manipulation has caused major exploits
• Extra complexity and cost for developers

In practice oracles become a fragile middleware layer and often a single point of failure.

This is why oracles are called a necessary patch not a clean solution.

3. How Rialo is different

Rialo is a next generation Layer 1 built as a real world blockchain.

Instead of adding oracles on top Rialo makes real world interaction a native feature of the protocol.

No external oracle networks required.

4. Native web access on chain

Rialo smart contracts can directly interact with the web.

• Contracts can make outbound HTTPS requests to public APIs
• External services can push data via inbound webhooks
• Contracts react to real world events instead of polling data

This turns the blockchain into an event driven system rather than a closed environment.

5. Trust without oracles using TEEs

Direct web access still needs security. Rialo solves this with Trusted Execution Environments.

• Web calls are executed inside secure hardware enclaves
• The enclave provides cryptographic proof that the data is real and untampered
• The proof is verified on chain

No oracle nodes. No separate consensus layer. Trust is minimized at the hardware level.

6. Built in real world primitives

Rialo removes more external dependencies.

• Native timers and schedulers no keepers or bots
• Event triggers for payments deliveries or price changes
• Real time reactions to market moves without lag

These features are part of the protocol not add ons.

7. Full stack performance design

Rialo combines multiple modern approaches.

• Parallel execution for high throughput
• RISC V architecture
• Solana VM compatibility
• Stake for Service converting staking yield into gas credits
• Built in privacy features

The result is a monolithic chain where everything works together by default.

8. Why this matters

This architecture changes what developers can build.

• No oracle manipulation attacks
• Fewer failure points
• Predictable costs
• Web2 like developer experience

Developers focus on logic not infrastructure glue.

9. Real world use cases unlocked

• Prediction markets that settle instantly
• RWAs with direct compliance and verification
• DeFi strategies reacting in real time
• Apps using payments identity and APIs natively

For users this feels like a normal app. Faster interactions fewer wallet interruptions and seamless flows.

Rialo is not just a faster blockchain.
It is a rethink of how blockchains should interact with the internet.

By making real world data native it removes the need for traditional oracles entirely and moves blockchain closer to mainstream usability.

Simply put: In blockchain, code must run identically on every validator — fast, predictably, and securely — even if it's malicious.
RISC-V is an open, clean real-CPU architecture that delivers:
- Fast & predictable single-pass compilation (no DoS via complex JITs)
- Top-tier tooling (LLVM, Rust, proper debugging/profiling)
- Compact binaries
- Easy compatibility with other VMs (SVM already supported, EVM/Move planned as guests)
- Built-in ZK-proof readiness & crypto flexibility
Unlike WASM (great for browsers, complex for chains), eBPF (kernel-focused, heavy toolchain), or EVM (legacy 256-bit stack model)—RISC-V strikes the perfect balance of performance, security, and future-proofing.

Today, I will explain this more simply using the café example we discussed previously.

Let us assume a café is a single network. This café has three core components.

First, hygiene and safety management, which corresponds to security in a blockchain. 

Second, ingredients and cash flow, which correspond to liquidity. 

Third, the menu, services, and physical space, which correspond to utility.

From a traditional perspective, operating a café means these elements are seen as conflicting with one another. Raising hygiene standards increases costs.
Stocking more ingredients ties up cash. Expanding menus and services increases operational complexity.

As a result, rewards are also simple: the more money you invest, the more profit you expect to earn.

However, under a superadditive perspective, the design changes.

Consider a situation where strengthening hygiene management does not end as a mere cost increase.

To improve hygiene standards, the café systematizes staff training.

Through this process, employees gain a deeper understanding of menu items and ingredient characteristics.

As a result, ingredient waste decreases and inventory turnover improves.

This directly leads to better liquidity efficiency.

At the same time, stable hygiene and operations increase customer trust.

As trust accumulates, repeat customers increase, and the café becomes able to introduce expanded utilities such as new menu items or subscription-based services.

These new services, in turn, create stable demand, making cash flow and inventory management more predictable.

The key point in this structure is that hygiene improvement, ingredient management, and service expansion do not generate rewards independently. Instead, they interact with one another and create additional value together.

In other words, a single action improving hygiene simultaneously promotes liquidity efficiency and service expansion.

At this point, the café’s performance is not the simple sum of hygiene, ingredients, and services. Because of their interaction, the outcome is greater than the total of the individual parts.

This is what is referred to as superadditivity in blockchain economics.

Actions that contribute to security lock liquidity. That liquidity, in turn, expands network utility.

Expanded utility then incentivizes further participation in security.

Rialo’s design philosophy does not focus on optimizing each element in isolation to grow the café. Instead, it begins by asking which combinations of operations reinforce one another.

As a result, as the network grows, complexity becomes a source of competitiveness rather than a burden.

This is why superadditivity is not merely a conceptual explanation, but the core design principle of the Rialo network economy.

From Passive Ledgers to Active Networks

How Rialo Frames the Shift

A ledger records what already happened.
An active network responds to what is happening.
That difference sounds subtle.
But it changes everything.

This distinction sits at the core of how Rialo defines the problem with today’s blockchains.

What a Ledger Can’t Do

A ledger is excellent at one thing.

Preserving history.

It can tell you:

Who sent what
When state changed
Why a transaction was valid

But it cannot:

Observe events
Anticipate outcomes
Coordinate actions across systems

It waits to be written to.

That’s not a flaw.
It is a design boundary.

And it is precisely the boundary Rialo argues Web3 never moved beyond.

Why Apps Outgrew Ledgers

Modern applications do not just record outcomes.
They react.

If a user clicks a button, something happens.
If a market moves, positions rebalance.
If a condition is met, logic executes immediately.

Web2 systems are active by default.

Blockchains are not.

So developers built layers on top.

Off-chain services
Bots
Keepers
Cron jobs pretending to be decentralization

The system works.
But the blockchain is no longer the system.

It becomes a settlement layer.

According to Rialo’s framing, this is where Web3 lost coherence.
Execution moved off-chain, while trust remained on-chain.

What Makes a Network Active

An active network is defined by one property.
Execution is driven by conditions, not transactions.

That means:

Logic can be bound to events
State can change when inputs change
Execution is continuous, not episodic

No one has to poke the system.

The system is already watching.

This is the execution model Rialo is built around.
Not faster transactions, but always-on logic.

This Is Not Automation

Automation still assumes:

Someone set it up
Someone maintains it
Someone fixes it when it breaks

Active networks are different.

They are designed so that:

Observation is native
Reaction is verifiable
Execution does not rely on babysitters

Less glue.
Less trust.
Less human intervention.

This distinction is central to Rialo’s design philosophy,
especially in contrast to bot-driven Web3 infrastructure.

Why This Changes What Blockchains Are For

Once a blockchain becomes an active network,
it stops being just a financial primitive.

It becomes:

A coordination layer
An execution fabric
A system that can enforce real-world logic

Not faster money.

Programmable reality.

This is the role Rialo claims blockchains were always meant to play,
but never structurally could.

The Shift Most People Miss

People ask:
Can this replace Ethereum?
Is this a Layer 1 or Layer 2?
Is it faster?

Those are ledger questions.

Active networks, including Rialo, answer a different one.

What should the system do when the world changes?

What Is a TEE, and Why Does @RialoHQ Start Here? 🔐

As mentioned earlier, Rialo is not chasing theoretically perfect privacy Instead, it aims to solve real privacy problems by adopting execution models that actually work in practice.

Real-World Services Are Built on Secrets ⚙️

The services we use every day are designed around sensitive information. If that information is exposed, the service itself cannot function.

However, traditional blockchains are built on an execution model where all inputs and computation are public by default.

➜ As soon as blockchains attempt to connect with the real world, they inevitably rely on off-chain servers, bots, and backends.

The blockchain is left as a ledger that merely records final outcomes 📒

TEE Fills This Gap Most Directly 💡

A Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) creates an isolated execution space inside the CPU, allowing computations to run while keeping sensitive data hidden from external observers.

As a result, TEEs:
👉 address privacy issues immediately
👉 and are already proven solutions widely used in real-world systems today

Why Rialo Treats TEE as a Core Pillar 🎯

Rialo believes that for blockchains to become a true component of real-world services, they must support real-time execution and secure external integration.

This means:
• Reacting instantly to price changes
• Executing logic the moment conditions are met
• Communicating safely with external systems

Judged purely by these requirements, TEE is the most practical option available today 🔗

• Latency: milliseconds
• Overhead: relatively low
• Web2 integration: immediately feasible

For this reason, Rialo actively uses TEEs as the foundation for AI agents, automated financial logic, and real-time trigger execution.

A Hybrid Privacy Architecture 🧠

That said, TEEs require a degree of trust in hardware vendors and manufacturers. Relying on a single TEE instance can also introduce centralization risks.

Rather than relying on a single, all-purpose privacy solution, Rialo treats TEE as a practical starting point for connecting blockchains to reality and layers multiple complementary technologies on top.

• Fast, real-time computation is handled inside TEEs
• Execution integrity is verified using ZKP
• Trust-sensitive segments are secured with MPC
• Extremely sensitive data is protected with FHE

In short, TEE provides realism and speed, while the other technologies exist to reinforce trust, decentralization, and long-term security.

If execution is distributed,
if ownership is shared,

It needs structure.

Web2 solves responsibility through hierarchy.

Someone owns the system.
Someone answers when things break.

Web3 removed the hierarchy —

Combining a photo with its location was nearly impossible or extremely complex. The smartphone integrated all of these functions in a supermodular way. When camera location and internet worked together without friction services like Uber and Instagram were born. This is the power of combinatorial innovation.

The future of blockchain will be judged by Time to Value which means how quickly an idea can become a real service. Supermodularity breaks down technical barriers and removes the Integration Tax. It allows blockchain to connect real world data and value organically.

Blockchain systems must coordinate economic interactions in which multiple components influence one another simultaneously.

In particular, how the relationships between security, liquidity, and utility are designed determines whether a network can remain stable and grow sustainably over time.

Traditional design approaches have treated these elements as separate components and attempted to optimize each one independently.

Under this framework, trade-offs were assumed to be inevitable: strengthening security increases costs, increasing liquidity weakens security, and expanding utility raises system complexity.

From this perspective, reward structures are also designed in a linear manner.

In other words, the more capital a participant deposits, the more rewards they receive.

However, Rialo points out that this linear approach fails to explain the economics of integration.

When designing its network economy, Rialo aimed to move beyond simple linear reward structures and instead create a system in which monetary reinforcement emerges through interaction.

The concept that arises from this line of thinking is superadditivity.

Security, liquidity, and utility are not treated as independent elements, but as complementary components whose values are amplified when they are strategically combined.

For example, if an action that contributes to network security simultaneously locks liquidity, and that liquidity is then used to expand network utility, participants gain economic benefits that go beyond simple rewards.

In this case, rewards are not generated by the sum of individual actions, but by the interactions created as those actions interlock.

Within this structure, strengthening one element does not mean sacrificing another.

Instead, as security improves, liquidity efficiency increases; as liquidity deepens, utility expands; and expanded utility, in turn, incentivizes further participation in security.

This mutually reinforcing cycle is what defines a superadditive network economy.

From Rialo’s perspective, the key question is not “how much reward is given,” but rather “which combinations create additional value.”

This design philosophy ensures that as the network grows, complexity becomes a competitive advantage rather than a burden.

As participation increases, the system does not merely grow in a linear fashion, but becomes structurally stronger and more useful.

In this sense, superadditivity can be understood not merely as an economic concept, but as a core design principle through which Rialo views and builds its network.

In the current Web3 architecture, most applications do not execute directly on the blockchain. Instead, they rely on a extensive stack of middleware components, including indexers for data querying, oracles for external data feeds, bots for automation tasks, RPC providers for network interactions, and relayers for transaction routing.

These components typically operate independently, each with its own lifecycle, latency characteristics, and fault-tolerance mechanisms. When any single element experiences delays, disconnections, or synchronization issues, it can interrupt the entire application flow, resulting in stalled operations, failed automations, and operational costs that scale disproportionately.

This complexity represents a significant “hidden cost” in Web3: the overhead that developers incur simply to maintain basic functionality.

Moreover, relying on multiple middleware layers increases system weight, enlarges the potential attack surface, and introduces additional points of failure.

Rialo addresses this challenge at the architectural level. Rather than shifting logic offchain and depending on external services, Rialo integrates key operational elements- such as data handling, execution, and automation- directly into the blockchain’s native environment, within a unified system.

This design seeks to minimize inter-component dependencies, reduce state inconsistencies, and potentially enable better operational continuity, lower latency, and a simpler trust model for applications.

Automation becomes an inherent part of the infrastructure, rather than relying on separate offchain scripts.

In summary: reduced middleware, fewer potential failure points, and a path toward more comprehensively onchain applications.

The Profitable Inefficiency

Right now, oracle delays create money making opportunities. When Chainlink or another oracle service updates a price feed even seconds after a real market move, arbitrageurs act. They know the on-chain price is stale, They know what the “real” price is and in that brief window of information asymmetry profits exist.

It’s a specific kind of arbitrage that lives entirely because of infrastructure limitations. DeFi protocols display prices that are objectively wrong for brief periods. Traders who monitor both traditional markets and blockchain price feeds simultaneously can exploit these discrepancies with near certainty. The oracle lag isn’t a bug for these traders; it’s the entire feature.

The traders who’ve built sophisticated systems to monitor oracle updates and execute against stale on-chain prices might find their edge gone.

This raises a genuine question: Is eliminating this opportunity a net positive?

🔻Most Web3 apps say they “integrate APIs”

Very few actually do it in a way the chain understands.
That difference matters more than it sounds.

🔹Traditional external APIs in Web3 work like this

The contract itself cannot reach the web.
So you run a backend, bot or oracle that calls an API, processes the response, then submits a transaction with a simplified result.

From the chain’s point of view, reality arrives late, filtered and pre-digested.
You are trusting the messenger more than the data.

🔹What native web calls actually change

With native web calls, the contract logic itself can pull data from external services during execution or as part of automated flows.
No relay server deciding when to push updates.
No custom glue translating responses into “oracle format”.
The chain is no longer waiting. It is actively querying.

That flips the model from “someone tells the contract what happened” to “the contract checks for itself”.

🔹Why this is not just about speed

Yes, native calls reduce latency.
But the bigger shift is architectural.
When contracts can access APIs directly, you can design logic around conditions, events and state transitions that live outside the chain.
Usage-based pricing, real-time risk checks, automated settlements, event-driven payouts all without building and babysitting a parallel backend.

Traditional APIs keep Web3 reactive.
Native web calls make it proactive.

🔹Where Rialo fits

Rialo treats web calls as a first-class primitive of the network.
They are not an add-on service or a workaround. They are part of execution and automation.

That means fewer hidden trust assumptions and fewer places where your product can quietly break offchain.
The app logic stays where it belongs: inside the protocol, not scattered across scripts and vendors.
The real question is not “can we call APIs”.
It is whether the chain is allowed to do it itself.

Execution That Doesn’t Wait

@RialoHQ

Most blockchains execute in the same way.

They wait.

A transaction shows up.
The contract runs.
State updates.
Then nothing.
Until the next transaction.
That model worked when blockchains were just ledgers.
It breaks once we expect them to behave like applications.
Because the real world does not wait.

The Passive Ledger Problem

Blockchains are built around a simple assumption.
Nothing happens unless someone submits a transaction.

Prices do not move.
APIs do not update.
Markets do not open or close.

Not until something from the outside pokes the chain.

That is why everything feels bolted on.

Oracles push data.
Bots trigger contracts.
Keepers watch state.

The chain itself stays passive.
Fast and secure.
Decentralized.
But always reacting after the fact.

This Is Not a UX Issue

When people say Web3 feels clunky,
they are not talking about block times.

They are feeling the gaps.

Between real-world events and onchain execution.
Between off-chain systems and onchain logic.
Each gap adds delay.
Each delay adds friction.
Each workaround adds trust.

You can polish interfaces forever.
A passive execution model will still leak complexity.

What Active Execution Means

Active execution is not about faster blocks.
It changes the question.
Instead of who will trigger this contract,
it asks what should happen when the world changes.

That implies continuous inputs.
Execution that reacts instead of waiting.
Verification instead of trust.

This is about what execution is allowed to see.

Why This Was Hard Before

Blockchains avoided this for good reasons.

Determinism mattered.
Consensus safety mattered.
Verifiability mattered.
Letting reality into execution felt risky.

So execution was sealed off
and reality was patched in through oracles.
That tradeoff is starting to break.
Not because systems trust more.
Because they can verify more.

Where Rialo Fits

Rialo starts from a different assumption.

Execution does not have to be passive.

It can observe, verify, and react
as part of the execution model itself.

Not a chain that waits to be told what happened.
A system designed to respond as it happens.

That does not replace blockchains.
It expands what they can do.

Execution that keeps up with reality.

트랜잭션은 시스템에 들어온 뒤 확정되거나 폐기될 때까지 여러 상태를 거친다. 이 과정에서 자원 소모와 지연이 발생하고, 상태 전이 지점에서 병목이 생기면 전체 시스템 성능이 떨어진다. Rialo는 각 단계의 상태 전이를 명확하게 정의하고, 합의 지연이나 I/O 병목을 최소화하는 구조를 채택했다.

특히 자원 경합은 실패의 주요 원인이다. 읽기 쓰기 충돌이나 락 경쟁은 실행 지연과 대기열 정체를 유발한다. Rialo는 다중 버전 제어와 행 수준 락을 통해 경합을 줄이고 교착 상태를 자동 탐지해 우선순위에 따라 처리한다.

지연은 단순히 느림의 문제가 아니라 실패의 전조다. 연결 풀 고갈, TCP 재전송, 컨테이너 스로틀링은 모두 트랜잭션 취소로 이어질 수 있다. Rialo는 하드웨어 자원 활용 최적화와 네트워크 토폴로지 설계를 통해 테일 레이턴시를 줄이고 시스템의 일관성을 확보한다.

복잡한 트랜잭션 흐름에서 실패한 단계를 보상하는 구조도 중요하다. Rialo는 이벤트 기반 아키텍처를 통해 보상 트랜잭션을 자동 실행하며, Saga 패턴을 지원해 시스템 정합성을 유지한다.

But execution quality depends on when information arrives.

1. Issues Criticized in the Post (Web3’s Hidden Tax) The post lists common middleware components in Web3 and their risks, leading to application freezes and automation failures. These are real-world problems in current blockchains like Ethereum or Solana, where developers rely on third-party services to connect on-chain with off-chain. 
- Indexers lag: Indexers (like The Graph) are used for fast on-chain data lookups, but they can be slow due to processing large amounts of data. Result: Applications cannot access data in a timely manner, leading to a poor user experience.
- Oracles break: Oracles (like Chainlink) provide off-chain data such as stock prices or weather, but they can fail due to data source errors or attacks. This is the well-known "oracle problem," posing risks to DeFi (e.g., incorrect liquidation).
- Bots fail: Bots (such as MEV bots or automation bots) are used to execute automated logic (e.g., arbitrage trades), but they can fail due to network congestion or software errors.
- RPCs timeout: RPCs (Remote Procedure Calls, like Infura) are gateways to the blockchain, but they can time out under high load, interrupting transactions.
- Relayers stall: Relayers (like Gelato) forward transactions or automation, but they can "stall" due to fluctuating gas fees or network errors.

Overall, the post calls this "middleware everywhere just to function" – a complex system with many weaknesses, increasing operating costs and reducing the reliability of dApps.

2. How Rialo Technology Solves It (With Rialo, it all goes native) 
Rialo is not an additional layer but an L1 designed from the ground up to integrate these functions into the core protocol, eliminating the need for middleware. This makes the system "unbreakable," with sub-second speeds and high automation. Below is a detailed analysis of how Rialo handles each problem: 
- Replacing indexers with native indexing: Rialo integrates indexing directly into the L1 architecture, using event-driven logic so that data is updated in real time without the need for external services. Developers can access data on-chain without lag, as everything happens within the same network.
- Eliminate oracles with native data fetching: Instead of oracles, Rialo allows fetching data directly from sources (e.g., APIs like weather or credit scores) via transaction triggers. No more "telephone game" (misinformation transmission) or stale data. For example, prediction markets can pull election or sports results on-chain without intermediaries.
- Bots and automation become native: Rialo uses Rialo Extended Execution (REX) to automate logic based on real-world events (e.g., market-triggered trades or subscriptions). Bots are no longer needed because contracts auto-trigger, reducing failures due to external errors.
- RPCs and relayers are natively optimized: With Solana VM-compatible architecture and RISC-V smart contracts, Rialo ensures smooth RPCs without timeouts, as all connections are intrinsic. Relayer stalls are avoided by making scheduling and execution part of the protocol, independent of third-party services.

Result: "No middleware. Real apps." Rialo reduces complexity by collapsing these layers into a single network, allowing developers to build applications such as tokenize RWAs (e.g., real estate, invoices), automate actions (e.g., event-based coupons), or bridge Web2/Web3 (e.g., email login).
This makes Web3 "invisible" - users don't perceive the complexity, similar to how the iPhone makes technology accessible.

Before starting this article, I first studied the ideas of supermodularity and economic interaction.

Supermodularity means that when two elements work together, they create more value than when each element is used separately and simply added together.

In mathematical form, it is written as
f(A + B) ≥ f(A) + f(B).
This means the two elements support each other and create synergy.
So instead of thinking 1 + 1 = 2, you can think of it as 1 + 1 ≥ 3.

For example, let A be data and B be an AI model.
Data alone has limited meaning, and an AI model alone has nothing to learn from.
But when data and an AI model are combined, they can create much greater value, such as prediction, automation, and decision-making.
This increase in value does not come from simply adding the performance of data and the model.
It comes from new effects that appear when the two are combined.

To explain this more easily, imagine running a café as the owner.
If one barista works alone, the café might sell 50 cups of coffee per day.
Adding a kiosk or another barista does not automatically increase sales to 100 cups.
Instead, when ordering and payment are separated, the barista can focus only on making coffee, and the café can end up selling 200 cups per day.
This kind of structure, where each element increases the efficiency of the others and total results grow much more than expected, is a supermodular structure.

Next, it is important to look at economic interaction.
Economic actors include individuals, companies, governments, platforms, and users or network participants.
Interaction means that my choices affect others’ choices, and their choices affect my results in return.

The stronger these interactions are, the more likely it is that acting together creates more value than acting separately.

In other words, economic interaction provides the foundation for supermodularity and is a key concept for understanding network economies.
So far, we have looked at why structures designed to work together can create more value than a simple sum.
When we apply this idea to blockchain systems, it becomes clear why designing security, liquidity, and utility separately has limits.
It also becomes clear why mutually reinforcing structures are so important in network economies.

In the next article, based on what we studied today, I will take a closer look at how supermodularity works as a design principle in Rialo.

Web3 is full of problems.

Scalability. Trust. UX. Coordination. Verification.
Every project claims to be solving at least three of them.
But this creates a quieter issue:

When everything is a problem, nothing is clearly owned.

In Web3, “problem statements” often become marketing lists.

The more problems a project claims to solve,
the harder it becomes to understand what it is actually responsible for.

This isn’t ambition.
It’s a lack of prioritization.

And without prioritization, roles collapse.

Web2 companies usually start by narrowing the problem:
- one job
- one responsibility
- one clear value proposition

The cost is centralization.

Web3 tried to do the opposite:
- open participation
- shared ownership
- composability

But many projects also expanded their problem scope at the same time.

The result:
- decentralization exists
- but responsibility is diluted

Users are left asking:
“What does this protocol actually take ownership of?”

@RialoHQ doesn’t try to solve everything.

some problems are worth structuring around — others are not.

This is an underrated design decision.

Choosing a problem defines:
- what the protocol is accountable for
- what it deliberately ignores
- and how success should be measured

Of course, this raises harder questions:
- Is the chosen problem truly fundamental?
- Does the ecosystem agree it’s worth solving?

Before asking how @RialoHQ solves things,
it’s worth asking what it believes is worth solving at all.

from role, to problem, to structure.

[ @RialoHQ Solution: Stake-for-Service (SfS) 🧐 ]

Rialo’s SfS allows staking rewards to be automatically used to pay transaction fees.

Here’s how it works, explained simply 🔍

🔸 Step 1: One-time setup when staking

➜ When you stake your tokens, you can predefine how your staking rewards will be used.

For example, you can set: “Automatically route 30% of my rewards to gas fees.”

Once set, there’s nothing more you need to manage.

This ratio where a portion of rewards is redirected to cover gas fees is called the routing ratio.

🔸 Step 2: Rewards are automatically converted into gas credits

➜ When staking rewards are generated, the portion defined by the routing ratio is automatically transferred to a gas-dedicated account.

These rewards are then immediately converted into service credits, which function as gas fee points.

It’s similar to how cash is automatically topped up onto a transit card.

🔸 Step 3: Credits are used automatically when you transact

➜ When you make transactions or use apps on the blockchain, there’s no need to check your wallet balance or prepare gas tokens separately.

Your accumulated service credits automatically pay the gas fees for you.

🔸 Step 4: Validators are still rewarded as usual

➜ Even though gas fees are paid using credits,
the validators who process transactions still receive their rewards in native tokens, just as before.

In other words, network security and the reward structure remain fully intact.

Key takeaway 👏

👉 Stake-for-Service removes the traditional separation where staking is treated as investment and gas fees as consumption, and instead creates a system where assets naturally and continuously sustain network services.

Rialo가 바꾸는 실행 레이어의 미래

블록체인의 병목은 더 이상 합의가 아니라 실행이다. 합의 알고리즘은 충분히 발전했고, 이제 진짜 경쟁은 트랜잭션을 얼마나 효율적으로 처리하느냐에 달려 있다. 전통적인 순차 실행 모델은 결정론적 안정성을 보장하지만, 멀티코어 하드웨어를 전혀 활용하지 못한다. 이로 인해 병목, 가스비 상승, 지연 시간 증가 같은 문제가 반복된다.

병렬 실행은 이런 한계를 극복하기 위한 방향이지만, 상태 경합과 비결정성이라는 위험이 뒤따른다. 사전 접근 경로를 명시하는 PCC 모델(Solana)과, 사후 충돌을 감지하는 OCC 모델(Monad, Aptos)은 각각 장단점이 분명하다. PCC는 빠르지만 개발자에게 부담이 크고, OCC는 호환성이 높지만 고경합 상황에서 성능이 급격히 하락한다.

Rialo는 여기에 반응형 실행이라는 완전히 새로운 모델을 제안한다. 사용자가 트랜잭션을 보내야만 작동하던 기존 구조와 달리, Rialo는 외부 이벤트나 내부 조건에 따라 자동으로 실행이 시작되는 구조다. 이는 스케줄링 권한이 사용자에서 프로토콜로 넘어간다는 의미이며, 충돌 가능성을 낮추고 병렬 처리의 안정성을 높이는 핵심 설계다.

또한 Rialo는 블록 체인 구조 대신 DAG 기반의 실행 그래프를 사용한다. 순서가 필요 없는 트랜잭션은 병렬로, 의존성이 있는 트랜잭션은 안전하게 순차 처리한다. 이를 통해 시스템 전체가 실제 데이터 흐름에 따라 최적화된다.

외부 데이터 오염, 비결정론적 API 응답, 상태 전이의 불확실성 등 병렬 실행의 고질적인 문제를 해결하기 위해 Rialo는 결정론적 래핑, 원자적 정산 같은 메커니즘을 도입했다. 이는 블록체인이 외부와 연결되면서도 내부 일관성을 잃지 않도록 설계된 중요한 안전장치다.

보안 측면에서도 Rialo는 단일 키 기반 보안에서 벗어나 임계치 키를 사용한다. 분산 키 생성과 MPC를 기반으로 한 이 구조는 키 분실이나 탈취에 강하며, 소셜 복구와 2FA도 가능하게 한다. 사용자는 이메일이나 소셜 로그인으로 손쉽게 온보딩하고, 복잡한 키나 시드 구문 없이도 안전하게 자산을 관리할 수 있다.

개발자 경험을 고려해 RISC-V 기반의 고성능 연산을 지원하고, Solana VM과 호환성도 제공한다. 기존 생태계에서 빠르게 넘어올 수 있도록 설계된 다리 역할을 자처한다.

Rialo가 특히 강점을 보이는 분야는 외부 데이터와 연결되는 예측 시장, 자산 토큰화, 자동화된 금융 서비스다. 오라클 없이 API 데이터에 반응해 자동으로 정산이 일어나고, 배당금 지급이나 청산 같은 과정도 외부 이벤트에 따라 안전하게 실행된다.

Oracles Didn’t Fix the Problem : They Hid It
@RialoHQ
When blockchains couldn’t see the real world,
we didn’t change the system.

We patched it.

We called the patch an oracle.

At first, it looked like a solution.
Smart contracts could finally react to prices, events, APIs, and outcomes beyond the chain.

But here’s the uncomfortable truth:

Oracles didn’t solve the blindness.
They outsourced it.

The Oracle Model Is Still a Closed World

An oracle does not make a blockchain aware of reality.

It does something much narrower:
• Someone watches the real world
• Someone decides what data matters
• Someone packages it
• Someone pushes it onchain

From the contract’s point of view, nothing changed.

It still lives in a closed, deterministic universe.
It just receives messages from outside.

That means the most important question is no longer cryptographic.

It’s social.
Who chose the data?
Who ran the oracle?
Who decided when reality mattered?

Complexity Didn’t Disappear  It Moved Off-Chain

Developers felt this first.

To make applications “work,” they added:
• Indexers
• Keepers
• Webhooks
• Cron jobs
• Monitoring scripts
• Fallback services

The dApp became an iceberg.

The onchain part looked clean and trustless.
The off-chain machinery grew massive, fragile, and opaque.

This is not decentralization.

It’s distributed trust with extra steps.

Why This Still Breaks at Scale

This model fails in predictable ways:

• Latency when reality moves faster than oracle updates
• Inconsistencies when different oracles disagree
• Silent failures when off-chain services go down
• Governance disputes over which oracle is canonical

These aren’t edge cases.

They’re structural.

Because the blockchain still cannot observe the world.
It can only be told about it.

The Question We Avoided

For years, the industry asked:
“How do we build better oracles?”
That was the wrong question.
The real one is:

Why is execution itself blind to the real world?

As long as execution lives in isolation,
no oracle can close the gap.
You can pipe reality in—
but the system was never designed to react to it natively.

Where @RialoHQ Reframes the Answer

Rialo starts from a different assumption:

What if execution was designed to see, verify, and react by default?

Not by bolting on middleware,
but by treating real-world signals as first-class inputs to execution itself.

In that model:
• Data arrives continuously, not episodically
• Execution reacts instead of waiting
• Verification replaces trust assumptions

That’s where this story is heading.

블록체인의 병목은 더 이상 '합의(consensus)'가 아니라 '실행(execution)'에 있습니다.
지난 10년이 PoW → PoS → PoH 등 합의 알고리즘의 시대였다면, 2025년은 실행 레이어의 경쟁이 생존을 결정짓는 해입니다. 왜 요즘 Rialo가 주목받고 있는지 분석해 봅니다.

왜 기존 체인은 느릴까? (EVM의 구조적 한계)
이더리움의 EVM은 10년 전 설계된 순차적 처리 방식을 유지합니다. 가장 큰 문제는 헤드오브라인 블로킹(Head-of-Line Blocking) — 앞선 트랜잭션이 완료되어야 다음이 실행됩니다. 이는 마치 8차선 고속도로에 톨게이트가 하나뿐인 구조로, 트래픽 병목과 가스비 폭등, UX 저하로 이어집니다.

Rialo isn't a Layer 1
Rialo는 단순한 L1 체인이 아니라, 프로그래밍 가능한 네트워크를 지향합니다. 오라클, 브릿지, 인덱서 등 외부 미들웨어 기능을 프로토콜 레벨에서 네이티브하게 통합함으로써, 복잡한 구성과 비용을 유발하던 ‘미들웨어 세금’을 제거했습니다. → 개발자 생산성과 체인 성능 모두 강화

핵심 기술 1: DAG & 병렬 실행
Rialo는 기존처럼 블록을 직선으로 쌓지 않고, DAG(Directed Acyclic Graph) 구조를 채택합니다. 의존성이 없는 트랜잭션은 병렬로 처리, 평균 지연 시간을 1초 미만으로 단축합니다.
수식으로 표현하면  Erialo≈EseqN+δE_{\text{rialo}} \approx \frac{E_{\text{seq}}}{N} + \deltaErialo​≈NEseq​​+δ → 처리 코어 수(N)가 많아질수록 성능이 기하급수적으로 향상됩니다.

핵심 기술 2: 반응형 스케줄링
기존 스마트 컨트랙트는 수동적입니다. Rialo는 이벤트 기반 실행 모델을 도입하여, 외부 신호나 API 호출에도 능동적으로 반응할 수 있습니다.
예: HTTP 요청 처리, 웹훅 반응 등 이를 통해 ‘반응형 클라우드’ 기능 구현 → 스마트 컨트랙트의 활용성이 대폭 확장됩니다.

UX 혁신: Threshold Key 기반 온보딩
복잡한 시드 구문? 이제 안녕입니다. Rialo는 Threshold Keys(임계값 키)와 분산 저장 기술을 활용하여, 사용자가 이메일이나 SMS 인증만으로도 지갑을 생성할 수 있는 Web2 수준의 온보딩 UX를 제공합니다.
사용자는 자기가 블록체인을 쓰고 있다는 사실조차 인식하지 못할 정도로 앰비언트(ambient) 환경을 경험하게 됩니다.

Stake for Service: A Better Way to Pay on Rialo

Staking on blockchains typically generates passive returns in exchange for network security. However, this return cannot be directly linked to actual transactions on the network, forcing users to make continuous manual payments for gas, storage or scheduled transactions. Rialo's SfS model offers a new economic architecture aimed at eliminating this disconnect.

✨SfS establishes an automated payment mechanism that directs the yield from staking directly to network services

✨A certain percentage of the yield generated from staked RLO is set aside for network services without going to the user's wallet.

✨This yield is converted into service credits via the ServicePaymaster component within the protocol.

✨Service credits are automatically spent on gas fees, storage, scheduled executions and continuously running contracts.

✨Manual balance management is eliminated, long running applications can self finance.

✨Staking transforms from a passive income tool into an active and continuous source of use.

The SfS model integrates security and usage costs within the same economic cycle at @RialoHQ. This approach enhances the network's sustainability while providing a predictable, automated and uninterrupted workflow for developers and applications. 
SfS plays a fundamental role in Rialo's economic design by making staking not just a lock up mechanism, but a direct mechanism for funding the network's operation.

At the heart of it is a simple but persistent issue: onchain systems are expensive to run and painful to manage.

The hidden cost problem in onchain systems: 

Onchain infrastructure depends on two very different types of capital. On one side, there is long-term staked capital locked up for security, alignment and rewards. On the other side, there are immediate, essential onchain costs like gas fees and rent that must be paid continuously in real time.

These two timelines don’t naturally align.

Because of this mismatch, teams are forced into a cycle of:
Volatile balances, where funds fluctuate unpredictably
Liquidity mismatches, where capital exists but isn’t usable when needed
Manual refueling and monitoring, requiring constant attention
And ultimately, the risk of halted operations if balances run dry
This isn’t just inconvenient, it creates real economic tension. Developers and users end up spending time managing wallets instead of building products. Reliability suffers and operational overhead quietly grows into a tax on innovation.

Instead of treating staking rewards and operational costs as separate systems, Rialo connects them through a stake-for-service (SFS) mechanism.

The underlying network continues minting staking rewards as usual

Instead of rewards sitting idle or requiring manual handling, they flow into the Rialo path.
Through the SFS mechanism, rewards are converted into credits
These credits create a continuous funding stream that automatically pays for onchain services
Smart contracts and dApps can then automate fees, removing the need for manual top-ups
The result is subtle but powerful.
From reactive management to predictable operations

Predictable, because funding is continuous

Hands-off, because manual refueling disappears

@RialoHQ the future of onchain infrastructure isn’t about adding more capital,it’s about using existing capital more intelligently.

Oracles exist for one reason:

Blockchains can’t see the real world.

So we introduced messengers.

The Promise of Oracles

In theory, oracles are straightforward.

They:
• Observe external data
• Deliver it onchain
• Let smart contracts react

Prices. Weather. APIs. Events.

At first glance, this seems sufficient.

The Structural Tradeoffs
Once a system depends on oracles, several structural costs emerge.

1) Latency Becomes Structural
Real-world data changes in milliseconds.
Oracles publish in batches, on schedules, or when thresholds are met.

This delay isn’t accidental.
It’s inherent to the design.

By the time data lands onchain,
the world has already moved.

2) Trust Re-enters the System
Most oracle systems rely on:

• Operator sets
• Multisigs
• Reputation systems
• Governance processes
These mechanisms are not cryptographic guarantees.
They are coordination assumptions.

For automated, high-stakes systems, that difference matters.

3) Costs Scale With Complexity
Custom feeds introduce recurring costs.
Teams pay:
• Per update
• Per feed
• Per day

And when updates fail to arrive on time,
downstream systems absorb the impact.

Why This Degrades Markets

In time-sensitive systems, delays compound quickly.
In derivatives and synthetic markets:

• Prices lag behind reality
• Liquidations trigger under outdated conditions
• Risk parameters drift out of sync

To compensate, teams introduce additional layers:

• Monitoring bots
• Safety margins
• Conservative configurations

Each layer protects the system
but reduces efficiency and UX quality.

Middleware Becomes the Norm

Oracles rarely operate in isolation.

They pull in:

• Indexers
• Automation bots
• Execution keepers
• Priority fee strategies

What begins as a single data feed
evolves into a network of interdependent services.

Development effort shifts
from product logic to infrastructure management.

Why Oracles Remain Widespread

Despite their drawbacks, oracles persist
because within the passive ledger model, there is no alternative.

If a chain cannot:

• Ingest external data natively
• Verify it cryptographically
• Compute over it continuously
• React deterministically

Then external coordination becomes unavoidable.

Oracles are not flawed solutions.
They are compensations for a deeper constraint.

In that model, oracle-style components still exist,
but they are no longer bolt-ons.

[ Parallel Execution and Object-Centric Models: Rialo’s Vision for a Conflict-Free Future ]

In the digital world the immediacy we enjoy is a carefully designed illusion. When we press like on Instagram or send money through a banking app we rarely feel the intense data battles happening behind the scenes. We only see a smooth message saying completed.

However, once we step into the world of blockchain and Web3, this illusion collapses.
Messages like “Transaction Failed” or “Network Congested” interrupt the experience.
As explained in Rialo’s research post A Visual Guide to Concurrency Control, these failures are not random bugs, but structural consequences of how a system treats time.

Most failures come down to order. Older blockchain designs look at the world in a sequential way. It is like every car in the world sharing a tunnel with only one lane. Even if the road is strong the moment the first car stops everyone else must stop too.

In this environment a simple transfer can be forced to wait because the single lane is already crowded with heavy traffic from other users. When a sudden surge of high volume activity occurs the entire path becomes blocked for everyone else. If this delay lasts too long the system triggers a timeout and the transaction is processed as a failure. This is the limit of sequential models and the main cause of the poor user experience we see today.

The parallel execution model creates thousands of lanes. It works like smart traffic control by predicting where each vehicle is going. By knowing which data will be used before starting the system processes many transactions at once. This prevents a single event from stopping the whole network.

As a result users are less likely to suffer from transactions failing because of invisible strangers. This is more than just a performance improvement. It is an attempt to change the very texture of the digital space.

To look deeper into the cause of failure we find two opposing philosophies. The pessimistic way locks data first which ensures safety but causes long waits. The optimistic way allows fast action but cancels the trade if a conflict is found at the last second. The failures we see are the price of this optimism. The system decides that going fast and failing occasionally is better than making everyone wait.

To fix this a model centered on objects is used. Instead of one big ledger the data is split into billions of independent pieces. Moving a coin in my pocket cannot physically touch someone else’s pocket.

Even if a conflict happens the system does not show a failure. It rebuilds the transaction in the background and tries again. The user only sees a smooth result.

Transaction failure is a signal from an old way of thinking that tried to force time into one line. The future vision is to change this narrow bridge into a wide plaza. Just as we do not think about power plants when using electricity users will not have to think about data locks. Transactions will simply flow.

In the end conflict free execution is not about removing complexity. It is about deciding where that complexity should live. 

Rialo does not eliminate concurrency or conflict. 
Instead, it moves them away from the user and into the system itself.

When infrastructure takes responsibility for time and order the user no longer has to.

Why Does Rialo Describe Itself as a “Role” Rather Than a “Product”?

Most Web3 projects explain themselves through features.

They tell us what they built, how fast it is, or how decentralized it claims to be.
But they rarely answer a more fundamental question:
What role does this project actually play in the ecosystem?

As a result, many projects end up competing in the same vague space —
part tool, part infrastructure, part service — without a clearly defined responsibility.

This isn’t a technical failure.
It’s a problem of role ambiguity.

In Web2, roles are clear.

Platforms, middleware, and service providers each have well-defined boundaries.
The trade-off is centralization and trust concentration.
Web3 tried to fix this by decentralizing execution and ownership.
But in doing so, many projects blurred their roles.

- Protocols act like products
- Products behave like infrastructure
- Infrastructure markets itself like consumer apps

The result:
 a system where decentralization exists, but responsibility does not.

This is why users often ask:
“What exactly does this project do for the network?”

Rialo approaches this problem differently.

Instead of starting with a list of capabilities,
it begins by defining the role it wants to occupy within the system.
That choice matters.

Defining a role sets:
- the scope of responsibility
- the limits of expansion
- and the expectations placed on the protocol

Rather than claiming to “solve everything,”
Rialo implicitly asks a narrower question:

Which responsibilities belong here — and which do not?

Of course, this also raises open questions:
- Can a role-first approach scale without becoming rigid?
- How does role clarity translate into real adoption?
- What happens when the ecosystem evolves faster than the role definition?

Rialo doesn’t fully answer these yet.
But the framing itself is notable.

Before evaluating whether Rialo succeeds,
it may be more important to ask whether its role is the right one to take on.
This research series starts there —
not with conclusions, but with structure.

🔹 What problem is Rialo solving?

Modern blockchains need parallel execution to scale but running transactions together can cause conflicts and incorrect results. Sequential execution is safe but too slow.

🔹 Why concurrency control matters

Concurrency control ensures that parallel execution still produces the same correct outcome as sequential execution. Without it, users face random failures, delays and poor UX during high activity.

🔹 Rialo’s approach

Rialo uses structured concurrency control to safely run transactions in parallel while preserving correctness (serializability).

🔹 Two execution models explained

Pessimistic execution: Prevents conflicts before execution. Safe but causes waiting and reduced throughput.

Optimistic execution: Executes immediately and fixes conflicts via retries. Faster and ideal when conflicts are rare.

🔹 Why optimistic execution fits Rialo

Rialo leans optimistic to maximize throughput, reduce latency and fully utilize modern hardware especially for real-world, read-heavy workloads.

🔹 The visual dashboard

The new dashboard makes these tradeoffs visible by showing transaction states (waiting, executing, rerunning, completed) in real time turning protocol theory into something intuitive.

🔹 What could come next

An adaptive execution model that dynamically switches strategies based on live network conditions could further improve performance without sacrificing safety.

🔹 Big takeaway

Rialo is not just scaling execution its designing predictable, user friendly performance that holds up as activity grows.

💎What is Stake-for-Service and why I paid attention to it

📌I’m sharing the Stake-for-Service model from @RialoHQ  because it shows a different way to think about staking in Web3. We usually treat staking as a source of passive income. You lock tokens in the network, receive rewards, and simply keep them in your wallet. But at the same time, you still pay for gas, storage, and operations separately, constantly monitoring your balance and topping it up manually.

📌This is where the problem appears. Rewards exist on their own, while network expenses exist separately. There is no connection between them. Because of this, automation slows down and the user experience becomes more complicated.

📌Stake-for-Service introduces a different logic. You create a position and define a portion of your future staking rewards that automatically goes toward paying for network services. Part of the yield doesn’t just accumulate. It is converted into credits that cover gas, smart-contract calls, and ongoing operations without manual top-ups.

📌You continue holding assets in staking, but at the same time you use part of the rewards as a working resource for the ecosystem. Processes don’t stop because of a missing gas balance, and the infrastructure is financed automatically from the same yield.

[@RialoHQ 's approach 🧡]

On most blockchains, smart contracts only execute when a transaction is submitted and terminate immediately afterward.

Under this execution model, the following behaviors are not handled naturally within the chain itself 📣
• Logic that waits until specific conditions are met
• Flows that resume execution after a certain amount of time
• Reactions to state changes in external systems

In other words, while the chain can compute what to execute when a request arrives, it does not, at the execution-model level, assume when execution should resume or which changes constitute meaningful events.

To fill this gap, Web3 applications have increasingly relied on off-chain middleware 🧩
• Indexers continuously track on-chain state
• Oracles relay data from outside the chain
• Bots and keepers monitor conditions and trigger transactions
• RPCs and relayers connect execution requests to the chain

All of these components take on responsibilities the chain itself does not natively perform: waiting, sensing, and re-executing.

As a result, applications evolve into structures where the chain and multiple off-chain components are linked in sequence.

If any one of these layers is delayed or fails, the entire application flow can come to a halt 🛑

This fragility is less a problem of individual middleware quality, and more a structural consequence of existing blockchain execution models,
which externalize these responsibilities by design.

Rialo takes a different approach.

Rather than making the middleware stack faster or more efficient, Rialo incorporates waiting on conditions, recognizing external events and resuming execution at the appropriate moment directly into the chain’s execution model as part of a natively continuous execution flow, rather than relying on external helpers 💫

In this context, what Rialo means by “No middleware” is not the elimination of all off-chain components, but a design choice to include by default roles that were previously forced outside the chain within the execution model itself.

As a result, the “Real apps” Rialo refers to are applications that:
• Do not depend on external monitoring logic
• Maintain uninterrupted execution and conditional flows
• Support automation in a structurally native way

This is where Rialo’s execution model diverges from existing blockchain architectures, and where the change Rialo proposes begins.

Stake-for-Service orientation Towards a self-sustaining on-chain economy where:

⚡️ Stake-for-Service (SfS): Turning Staking from "Passive Savings" into "Active Flow"

Rialo solves one of the biggest frictions in blockchain: the gap between capital and consumption. Traditionally, users stake tokens to earn yield but must keep separate balances to pay for gas.

Rialo’s SfS bridges this gap.

How does SfS work?

- Instead of letting staking rewards sit idle, SfS allows you to route a fraction of your yield directly into Service Credits.

- Automation: Your rewards automatically convert into "vouchers" that pay for gas, storage, and onchain tasks.

- Closed Economic Loop: Your capital secures the network while the yield it produces powers your activity no manual top-ups required.

Why is this a Game Changer?

- Gasless Onboarding: Apps can stake on behalf of users, letting them transact immediately without needing to buy tokens for fees first.

- "Forever" Contracts: Smart contracts can self-fund their recurring operations (like vault rebalancing) indefinitely using their own staking yield.

- Self-Updating NFTs: Dynamic NFTs can pay for their own metadata updates forever, funded by an initial stake.

- Predictable Budgeting: DAOs and enterprises can set fixed operating budgets based on yield fractions, removing the stress of token price volatility.

The digital continent we call Web3 is in reality less of a mainland and more of an archipelago composed of thousands of isolated islands. While Ethereum, Solana, and countless Layer 2s and app chains have established their own territories, the paths between these islands are far from smooth. 

To move data or transfer value, we have been forced to build numerous bridges through middleware such as oracles, indexers, and RPCs. 
However, Rialo offers a sobering insight into these precarious crossings. The very infrastructure we built to connect the space has become a hidden tax on Web3 that hinders innovation and erodes trust.

Today’s Web3 developers spend more energy patching system flaws than creating intrinsic value. The reality is that developer capacity is consumed by writing glue code to force different chains together and managing complex operations rather than building new features. 

This is in effect a harsh tax on innovation. This tax is not just about gas fees or commissions. Every time a layer of middleware is added, latency increases, points of failure multiply, and the cost of trust for the user rises.

The middleware we once considered essential has paradoxically become a shackle. When an indexer fails to sync, the app interface goes silent. When an oracle lags, a protocol decision making process slows down, often leading to catastrophic financial losses. 

We preach decentralized automation, yet we remain tethered to the stability of off chain bots and keeper servers. Our reliance on a few giant RPC providers threatens the core value of censorship resistance. Bridges in particular have proven through numerous exploits to be nothing more than fragile rope bridges in a storm, leaving users in constant anxiety.

This is where Rialo declares a fundamental redesign of the architecture. Rather than simply becoming another fast chain, Rialo proposes a chain native approach that absorbs the functions previously handled by middleware directly into the protocol. 

The core idea is not to pile on more features, but to bring the roles that were clumsily supported outside the chain back into the heart of the system.

At the center of this technical shift is the goal of direct connection to the external world. Rialo envisions a path where smart contracts interact with external services without relying on separate intermediate layers. The developer experience becomes as simple as a function call with results processed in a way that is verifiable at the protocol level. 

Furthermore, automation features like conditional execution or scheduling are handled within the protocol itself rather than depending on the survival of specific bot servers. The attempt to handle the states of fragmented chains as a single flow is a key design choice that finally allows developers to escape the trap of bridges and indexers.

Ultimately, these changes will open the era of Real Apps. These are applications that users can navigate without even realizing they are on a blockchain. Burdensome procedures like wallet connection, gas calculations, and network switching will vanish from the front end. 

Users will be left with seamless interfaces akin to Apple Pay or Instagram. In an environment where fragmentation is minimized, assets and data move naturally. Apps interacting with real world services through authenticated methods become a reality. As social triggers lead to automated execution and real world data is reflected without delay, blockchain will finally move beyond the confines of finance and become a functional part of daily life.

Perhaps middleware is a product of a transition period, much like the dial up modems of the early internet. Just as the static of the modem faded when broadband networks arrived, Web3 must strip away the opaque shroud of middleware and evolve into a system directly connected to the world. 

The innovation through removal proposed by Rialo is an attempt to reduce the heavy costs we have paid for the ideal of decentralization and to build Real Apps on a much firmer foundation.

When the static of the modem fades, the everyday reality of Real Apps will finally begin. In a world where technology does not have to struggle to prove itself, the future of Web3 envisioned by Rialo lies in that quiet yet powerful connectivity.

To understand why @Subzero_Labs chose RISC-V for @RialoHQ, you need to see what they rejected. Three major alternatives exist in blockchain, and each has a fatal flaw that would have prevented Rialo from becoming a real world internet-scale network.

1. The Ethereum Virtual Machine :

 That is the engine behind @ethereum, BSC, and @0xPolygon. 
It runs on a 256-bit stack-based architecture while modern hardware uses 64-bit systems. This mismatch creates a translation problem.

Every smart contract on the EVM must be heavily converted to work with actual computer processors. Complex operations like AI computations or advanced cryptography become painfully slow and expensive. For a blockchain trying to handle real world data at internet speed, this bottleneck would be fatal.

2. WebAssembly :
That is used by @Polkadot and @NEARProtocol. It was designed to run code in web browsers, which makes it fast for certain tasks. However, WASM is a high-level software abstraction not built for low-level hardware verification.

This matters enormously for privacy. Rialo uses Zero-Knowledge proofs to process sensitive data without revealing it. RISC-V instructions are so simple and direct that they can be proven mathematically with extreme efficiency. Vitalik Buterin and other experts have noted that RISC-V can be up to 100x more efficient for ZK proofs than other virtual machines.

If Rialo had chosen WASM, its privacy features would crawl at impractical speeds. The architectural simplicity of RISC-V makes cryptographic verification dramatically faster.

3. MoveVM :
That powers @SuiNetwork and @Aptos. Interestingly, some Subzero Labs founders previously worked on these projects. Move is exceptionally secure with strong safety guarantees, but it operates as a walled garden.

To build on Move, you must learn the Move programming language. This creates a severe developer bottleneck. The global pool of Move developers numbers in the thousands at most.

By choosing RISC-V, Rialo opens its platform to millions of existing Web2 engineers who already know C, C++, and Rust. These languages compile directly to RISC-V instructions. This decision transforms Rialo's potential developer ecosystem from a small niche community into a massive existing workforce.

Here is what Rialo gains from RISC-V compared to the alternatives:

• Language flexibility : 
Any language that compiles to RISC-V works natively, versus being locked into Solidity or Move

• Privacy performance : Hardware-native ZK proofs run exponentially faster than high-level VM implementations

• Real world connectivity : 
The chip-level architecture handles external data more naturally, enabling native webhooks without oracle overhead

• Execution speed : 
Operates at internet scale rather than traditional blockchain speed, processing real world events in real time

The key insight is that RISC-V is not just another virtual machine. It is an actual hardware instruction set that real processors understand. By building Rialo on RISC-V, Subzero Labs created a blockchain that thinks like a computer chip rather than like a sandboxed virtual environment.

This architectural choice explains how Rialo can communicate with external APIs directly, respond to real world triggers instantly, and process private computations efficiently. The blockchain operates at the same logical level as the hardware it runs on.

Without RISC-V, Rialo would face the same limitations as every other blockchain: isolated from the internet, slow at cryptography, and accessible only to specialized developers. The open source hardware architecture removes all three barriers simultaneously.

What @RialoHQ is actually trying to change: The Execution Model 🧐

Rialo does not see the core problem of blockchains as merely poor UX or developer friction.

➜ The problem, as Rialo defines it, lies in the execution model of blockchains themselves.

Traditional blockchains only operate when someone submits a transaction. they function as passive ledgers systems that react, record, and then immediately stop.

In other words, existing blockchains are characterized by:
• Execution only when a transaction is submitted
• Immediate termination once the transaction finishes
• No native concept of waiting, condition evaluation, or continuous logic
• Fundamental difficulty in expressing time-based logic, event-driven execution, or automatic reactions to real-world data directly on-chain

🔍Passive Ledger ➜ Active Network 🔍

Rialo redefines the blockchain not as a passive ledger, but as an always on network an Active Network 💫

The real world is constantly changing. It continuously generates events, signals, and data.

Yet traditional blockchains have treated reality as something that only matters after the fact something to be recorded once an outcome is finalized.

Rialo flips this model.

Instead of the network waiting for reality to be manually pushed in, the network should be able to observe reality, evaluate conditions, and progress autonomously to the next action when those conditions are met.

This shift is not about higher TPS or adding new features. It is closer to a redefinition of what a blockchain is capable of being.

🔻Are we actually ready for real-time APIs on a blockchain, or do we just like saying the phrase?

Everyone nods when they hear “real-time data”,but most of the current stack is built around something else entirely: delayed oracles, batch jobs and protocols that assume the world changes slowly

🔹What “real-time” really implies

Real-time is not “we update the oracle every minute”
It means contracts can:
-pull fresh data from external services during execution
-react to events as they happen, not hours later
-coordinate actions across users and systems with minimal lag

That is a different mental model from “submit a transaction and hope the next price update is close enough”

🔹Why the current stack can’t really do it

Today, “real-time” is faked with bots, keepers, offchain backends and aggressive polling.
You end up with:

-oracle networks pushing snapshots on a schedule
-automation scripts watching for conditions and then sending transactions
-apps that quietly accept that onchain state is always behind reality

It works for speculation. It breaks when the product depends on timing, SLAs or real business operations.

🔹What changes with a data-native L1

A chain like Rialo starts from a different baseline.
Contracts can call web APIs natively, use real-world data as first-class input and drive automation directly from those signals.

That unlocks things like instant risk checks, event-driven payouts or usage-based billing without building a custom automation stack on the side. The “API” is not a marketing line, it is part of the execution model.

🔹Why the market might not be ready

The hard part is not just infra.
Real-time APIs also demand:
-better risk and data models
-ops teams comfortable with continuous signals, not daily batches
-builders who design around behaviour instead of static snapshots

If you are not ready for that, a real-time chain will just expose how approximate your product always was.

So the question is honest, not rhetorical
Are you actually ready for applications that mirror reality in near real time
Or is “real-time onchain APIs” still more comfortable as a buzzword than as a design constraint

📋Why Stake-for-Service Is Necessary and Why This Structure Works Naturally on Rialo
The same issue keeps recurring across blockchains.

Users stake tokens to secure the network and earn rewards, but when it comes time to actually use services, they still need to manage separate balances
for gas fees and operational costs.

In this structure,
long-term locked capital and
day-to-day usage costs
are not naturally connected.

Rialo approached this problem not at the usage layer,
but at the design layer.

Rialo is a chain designed with continuously running services in mind.
When conditions are met, execution is triggered automatically, and recurring tasks and automation
are designed to function as native features of the chain.

In other words, on Rialo, execution is not an optional add-on, but a foundational assumption.

But if execution is the default, the payment model must evolve accordingly.

Continuously operating services require predictable and long-term payment structures.
Manual top-ups and reliance on volatile balances
make it difficult to sustain such systems reliably.

This is where Stake-for-Service (SfS) comes in.

SfS is a mechanism designed to allocate a portion of staking rewards toward paying for network services.

Instead of being treated solely as yield accumulated in a wallet, staking rewards can function as service credits
used to cover costs such as gas, storage, and scheduled execution.

Through this structure,
the burden of directly managing separate gas balances
can be significantly reduced for users.

As a result,
onboarding experiences that do not require direct gas purchases become possible, contracts can be designed to run over long periods based on a single staking position, and DAOs or institutions can construct models
that sustainably support user activity through staking.

Security and usability are no longer opposing forces,
but can scale together in the same direction.

On most chains, staking primarily serves as a way to accumulate yield.

On Rialo, however,
staking functions as a resource that enables execution.

Stake-for-Service is the structure that connects
staking and usage into a single flow, ensuring that execution can continue without interruption.

Closing Thoughts
What stood out to me was that Stake-for-Service did not feel like a newly invented revenue model,
but rather a way of resolving long-standing friction at the design level.
Seeing this structure made it clear why the separation between staking and usage has remained a persistent problem.
It finally made sense in a very natural way.

While organizing these thoughts, I realized that Stake-for-Service is less about earning more rewards
and more about ensuring that execution does not break or stop.
That distinction felt like a key point in truly understanding what Rialo is trying to achieve.

RISC-V is an open source instruction set architecture that is transforming how we build computer processors. Unlike ARM or x86 which require expensive licensing fees, RISC-V is completely free to use and modify.

The name breaks down simply. RISC stands for : 
Reduced Instruction Set Computer.

 A design philosophy where processors use fewer, simpler instructions to execute tasks faster and more efficiently. The V represents the fifth generation of RISC research from UC Berkeley.

What makes RISC-V revolutionary is its open nature. Any company or developer can take the base design and customize it for their specific needs without paying royalties or asking permission. This has made it popular for embedded systems, IoT devices, and increasingly for blockchain applications.

@RialoHQ, built by @Subzero_Labs, uses RISC-V as its core execution environment. This choice fundamentally changes what developers can do on a blockchain.

On traditional blockchains like Ethereum, you are locked into a custom virtual machine and specific programming languages. Rialo's RISC-V foundation means developers can write smart contracts in standard languages like Rust, C, or C++ and run them directly on the network.

The performance benefits are significant. RISC-V was designed for efficiency, allowing Rialo to achieve speeds comparable to standard web applications rather than the slower transaction times typical of many blockchains.

Rialo also maintains compatibility with the Solana VM, letting developers port existing Solana applications while gaining access to Rialo's real world integration features.

These real world features include native webhooks for making HTTPS calls to external APIs without requiring oracle services, event driven triggers that execute automatically based on real world conditions, and built-in privacy layers using advanced cryptography.

The result is a blockchain that can interact with external data sources, respond to real world events, and process sensitive information without the usual limitations or costly third party infrastructure.

Subzero Labs raised $20 million in 2025 from Pantera Capital and Coinbase Ventures to build this RISC-V powered infrastructure. The founding team includes veterans from Mysten Labs, Meta's Diem project, and Netflix.

By choosing RISC-V as its foundation, Rialo demonstrates how open source hardware architectures can unlock new possibilities for blockchain technology and bridge the gap between decentralized networks and real world applications.

The Stake-for-Service (SfS) model introduced by $Rialo is a rethink of how users pay for blockchain services.
Instead of treating staking and fees as two completely separate things Rialo connects them into a single self-sustaining system.

In simple terms:
Your staking rewards can be routed to automatically pay for network services without having to manage balances or manually top up fees.

On most blockchains today users must deal with two disconnected responsibilities:-

1)Stake tokens → to secure the network or earn yield
2)Hold liquid tokens → to pay for gas, storage, scheduled transactions, or recurring actions

This creates friction:

1) Wallets must be constantly monitored
2) Fees must be manually refilled
3) Long-running apps can fail just because fees run out
4) New users find the experience confusing and fragile

Staking helps the network but it does not help users use the network.

Rialo’s Core Idea: Turn Yield Into Utility

$Rialo flips this model with Stake-for-Service users can route a portion of their staking rewards into service credits that automatically cover network costs like:

1) Transaction execution
2) Storage
3) Scheduled or recurring operations
4) Ongoing smart contract activity

Your capital stays staked.
Your yield stays productive.
Your services keep running automatically as long as staking rewards are active.

1) You stake Rialo tokens
2) You choose what fraction of your staking rewards goes to services
3) That yield is converted into service credits
4) These credits automatically pay for network usage

No manual fee payments.
No constant balance checks.
No failed operations due to empty wallets.

Based on an interview with @itachee_x featuring @RialoHQ , I’ve prepared a recap that organizes the core questions Rialo raises and the direction it proposes.

The discussion can be broadly divided into three parts:
• Why existing blockchains still fail
• What Rialo is actually trying to change
